that they could “[c]ancel anytime,” followed by blue hyperlinked text reading “Learn
more.”…

                                            III…

“While new commerce on the Internet has exposed courts to many new situations, it has not
fundamentally changed the principles of contract.” “One such principle is the requirement
that ‘[m]utual manifestation of assent, whether by written or spoken word or by conduct, is
the touchstone of contract.’ “

Because contract formation is a question of state law, we first look to the appropriate state
law. The parties have represented that there are no material differences in the law of
contract formation in California, New York, North Carolina, and Florida (Plaintiffs’ states
of residence), and that California law should accordingly apply. And we have consistently
stated that no differences exist in the law of the different states as to internet contract
formation.

                                              A

In California, “internet contracts are classified ‘by the way in which the user purportedly
gives their assent to be bound by the associated terms: browsewraps, clickwraps,
scrollwraps, and sign-in wraps.’ “ Here, a link to the Terms of Service was provided to
Plaintiffs but they were not required to separately indicate that they had read or agree with
those terms before using justanswer.com’s services. Instead, they purportedly manifested
agreement by signing up for or continuing to use justanswer.com. So we employ the
inquiry-notice “sign-in wrap” analytical framework.

Under an inquiry theory of notice, contracts are formed between website users and
operators only where “(1) the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to
which the consumer will be bound; and (2) the consumer takes some action, such as clicking
a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests his or her assent to those terms.”

The first step of the inquiry-notice internet contract formation test asks whether “the
website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to which the consumer will be
bound.” This test has two aspects: the visual design of the webpages and the context of the
transaction. Both aspects “should be considered together.” This means that courts should
expect that a reasonable internet user is more vigilant in looking for contractual terms
when the context of the transaction reasonably implies a contractual relationship.




                                              63.
a
Consider first visual conspicuousness. For the most part, this is a matter of whether an
advisal is “displayed in a font size and format such that the court can fairly assume that a
reasonably prudent Internet user would have seen it.” This largely centers on an analysis of
the “visual aspects of the notice” within the “overall screen design.” This is necessarily a
visual and aesthetic analysis.

Under California law, this inquiry is “fact-intensive” and is informed by the “totality of the
circumstances.” Following California caselaw, we have discussed certain factors relevant to
our visual analysis of webpages and hyperlinks, such as the location of the advisal on the
webpage or the font size, color, and contrast (against the page’s background).

But we have not created a checklist for website designers. Nor have we generated per se
design rules that must be followed for a contract to be formed between a website user and
provider. “[T]here is no bright-line test for finding that a particular design element is
adequate in every circumstance.” And, by the same logic, there are not per se rules about
what’s necessarily inadequate, either. Such a one-size-fits-all approach would undermine
the fact-intensive, totality-of-the-circumstances nature of the analysis. Barring changes to
state-law doctrines regarding internet contract formation, any suggestion that hard-and-
fast rules constrain this inquiry results from over-reading or misreading our precedent.
Importantly—again, at least under California law— “even minor differences” in the design
elements may make the difference in this fact-intensive analysis. At bottom, when visually
analyzing the conspicuousness of an advisal and any hyperlinks, courts must be tuned to
the expectations of a reasonably prudent internet user. A hefty dose of common sense goes a
long way.

b
Together with the visual prominence of an advisal, we also consider under the first step the
“full context of the transaction,” such as whether the type of transaction “contemplates
entering into a continuing, forward-looking relationship” that would be governed by terms
and conditions. Following California caselaw, we have considered, for example, (1) whether
the transaction contemplates a “continuing relationship” by creating an account requiring a
“full registration process”; (2) whether the user is entering a “free trial”; (3) whether a user
enters “credit card information”; and (4) whether the user has downloaded an app on their
phone (suggesting consistent accessibility).

The second step of the inquiry-notice internet contract formation test asks us to consider
whether any action taken by the internet user—such as clicking a button or checking a
box—”unambiguously manifest[ed] his or her assent” to proposed contractual terms.

Following California caselaw, we have held that such unambiguous manifestation of assent
can only occur in the inquiry-notice context where an internet user is “explicitly advised
that the act of clicking will constitute assent to the terms and conditions of an agreement.”
Even strongly implicit advisement isn’t enough—a webpage must explain that certain
actions will be understood by the offeror to signal assent to contractual terms.

And it must identify what, exactly, those actions are. Chabolla, relying on California law,
emphasizes that the explanation of the legal significance of an action must truly be
unambiguous: there, an advisal read “[b]y signing up you agree ....” Because the action


                                               64.
button read “Continue,” however, rather than “Sign up,” the court concluded that there was
no unambiguous manifestation of assent. Explicit advisement generally looks like an
explanatory clause, usually at the beginning of an advisal—for example: “By clicking the
Continue >> button, you agree to the Terms & Conditions,” or “By tapping ‘Play’ I agree to
the Terms of Service”.

                                              B

With these standards in mind, we turn to the screens that Plaintiffs encountered to
consider whether any Plaintiff was put on inquiry notice that the use of justanswer.com
constituted agreement to the website’s Terms of Service. We conclude that none was. Some
Plaintiffs were presented with advisals that were insufficiently conspicuous to put them on
inquiry notice. Others weren’t explicitly advised of what actions would be taken to signal
assent to contractual terms. Thus, as we conclude below, no Plaintiff agreed to arbitrate a
claim.

1
First, consider Plaintiff Davis [Screen B]. The district court correctly determined that the
payment page that Plaintiff Davis saw did not put her on notice of any contractual terms.
The advisal text is printed in relatively small text and not located “directly above or below”
the action (“Start my trial”) button. This creates the impression of being visually “buried.”

Additionally, the color of the advisal text blends into the background and is displayed in a
lighter color than other text on the page. In fact, portions of the text are hard to read as
they do not contrast with the lighter portions of the background image. This gray-on-gray
presentation also suggests that the advisal is inconspicuous, and we would not expect a
reasonable internet user’s attention to be drawn to it. While each of these factors may not
be enough on their own to support Plaintiff Davis’s argument, under the totality of the
circumstances, the advisal was not visually conspicuous.

Furthermore, the context of the transaction is informed by the fact that there is an
automatically renewing subscription at issue. Under Sellers, automatic renewal
transactions are those where consumers make a one-time purchase of a product, which
triggers an “automatically recurring membership[ ]” for continued access to the product.
For such transactions, it must be clear that consumers agree not only to the one-time
purchase, but also to the continuing purchases going forward. In fact, Sellers considered not
only this sort of transaction, but a near-identical transaction involving the same website
and subscription.

2
As for Plaintiff Nelson [Screen C], the issue of gray-on-gray text has been cured and, unlike
the page that Plaintiff Davis saw, the advisal text is the same color as other text on the
page. The advisal is not, however, located directly above or below the action button and is
displayed in relatively small text. Considering the notice in the full context of the
transaction, we would not expect a reasonably prudent internet user to be on inquiry notice
of the contract.




                                              65.
3
Finally, we consider Plaintiffs Godun, Faust, and McDowell. Looking at the payment pages
that these Plaintiffs saw [Screens D & E], we need not consider step-one reasonable
conspicuousness. The advisal on these pages failed to explicitly advise users of what action
would constitute assent to any terms they were provided with. “The parties’ outward
manifestations must show that the parties all agreed ‘upon the same thing in the same
sense,’ “ and “[i]f there is no evidence establishing a manifestation of assent to the ‘same
thing’ by both parties, then there is no mutual consent to contract and no contract
formation.”

The advisal lacked an explanatory phrase indicating that “By clicking connect now” or “By
connecting,” or “By chatting,” etc., she agreed to the terms. Like the faulty advisals in
Berman and Chabolla, it instead simply said “I agree” without explaining more. Under our
precedent construing California law, that is not enough to constitute “an unambiguous
manifestation of assent” to those terms. And JustAnswer’s proposed routes around Berman
and that ambiguity are unavailing.

JustAnswer first suggests that Berman was not sufficiently clear on this point, or that no
such rule demands explicit advisement. While Berman was straightforward, we clear up
any remaining confusion: an advisal that simply states that “I understand and agree to the
Terms and Conditions” but fails to “indicate to the user what action would constitute
assent” is not enough to invite an unambiguous manifestation of assent.

Second, JustAnswer argues that “the full context of the transaction” should overcome the
lack of an explanatory “By clicking ... “ clause. But that argument misunderstands the
nature of the test and crosses doctrinal wires. The context of the transaction is relevant at
step one of the inquiry-notice online contract formation test, not step two. Again, step one
asks whether “the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to which the
consumer will be bound,” considering both visual conspicuousness and the context of the
transaction in totality. Step two asks a different question: whether there is an
unambiguous manifestation of assent. Step two does not look to the context of the
transaction but relies on the explicit advisement of what actions will be taken to signify
assent.

Relatedly, the parties trade volleys about whether the naked text overlaying an action
button can (or should) be dispositive. Under Chabolla, the text on an action button matters
insofar as it matches an advisal’s explanation. But nothing about the text on an action
button by itself can overcome the rule, in the inquiry-notice or “sign-in wrap” context,
mandating explicit advisement in advisal language so that there is unambiguous
manifestation of assent.

Accordingly, even if Plaintiffs saw these advisals, there was no meeting of the minds under
our precedent, and the payment pages that Plaintiffs Godun, Faust, and McDowell saw fail
at step two.

And the landing page that Plaintiff Godun saw [Screen A] was insufficient at step one to
put her on inquiry notice of JustAnswer’s proposed contractual terms. The advisal is
displayed in small text. Although the white text stands out against a black background and
is close to the action (“Start chat”) button, the black background is outside the main frame


                                             66.
of the screen. Placing the notice on the black border (coupled with an “x” button apparently
permitting the user to close a dialogue box) creates the visual impression of being “tucked
away” or not important to the transaction. While the page is generally uncluttered, the
placement of the advisal on the black border creates an impression of visual discontinuity.
This does not “capture the user’s attention” and direct her to the notice….

NELSON, Circuit Judge, concurring [with himself]*

… There’s no checklist, magic recipe, or set of per se rules to consult [regarding visual
conspicuousness]…I would conclude that the payment pages that Godun, Faust, and
McDowell saw [Screens D & E] satisfied the step-one visual-conspicuousness inquiry. After
all, if an internet user did not recognize that this underlined text is a hyperlink, she is not
reasonably prudent:




…[with respect to an unambiguous manifestation of assent], we demand magic words—or,
at least, we come very close. While this has the benefit of a bright-line rule, it is
inconsistent with historical and traditional contract law…

The Second Circuit has avoided this pitfall and correctly suggested that California law (and
the law of other states) wouldn’t demand these magic words. See Edmundson v. Klarna,
Inc., 85 F.4th 695 (2d Cir. 2023). Keeping with traditional principles of contract law, the
Second Circuit held that “acceptance need not be express,” and can be manifested by
“evidence that the offeree knew or should have known of the terms and understood that
acceptance of the benefit would be construed by the offeror as an agreement to be bound.”
Accordingly, the Second Circuit has held that an advisal beginning with “I agree ...” and
lacking any “By clicking ...” explanatory clause satisfies the step-two inquiry for a
comparable sign-in wrap agreement context—even under California law….

We got it wrong, the Second Circuit got it right, and we should pivot to follow its lead by
revisiting Berman’s explicit advisement rule.

                                        NOTES AND QUESTIONS

Whew, there is a lot going on here! These Notes and Questions should help you unpack
these opinions, but there is a lot to work through.


* [Editor’s note: Judge Nelson wrote the Godun majority opinion. Apparently, he didn’t agree with everything he

wrote, but he felt constrained by precedent. In his self-concurrence, he explains some of his divergent views.
Self-concurrences (writing a concurrence to a majority opinion the judge also wrote) are rare, but they are
popping up more frequently, especially among judges appointed by Pres. Trump.]



                                                        67.
Nomenclature Note #1: Assume the following terms are synonyms: user agreement, member
agreement, subscriber agreement, terms of use (TOU), terms of service (TOS), end user
license agreement (EULA), terms and conditions (T&Cs), and acceptable use policy (AUP).
This book uses these terms interchangeably. You’ll encounter many other synonyms in the
field.

Nomenclature Note #2: The “—Wrap” Taxonomy. The Chabolla opinion organized the
options for online contract formation into a four-node taxonomy:

     Term                                 Ninth Circuit’s Definition
 “Browsewrap”      “the user accepts a website’s terms of use merely by browsing the site,
                   although those terms are not always immediately apparent on the
                   screen. Courts consistently decline to enforce browsewraps”
 “Clickwrap”       “the website presents its terms of use in a pop-up screen and the user
                   accepts those terms by clicking or checking a box stating she agrees.
                   Courts routinely enforce clickwraps”
 “Scrollwrap”      “the user must scroll through all the terms before the website allows
                   her to click a box to agree…[this] provides the strongest notice and are
                   usually enforced”
 “Sign‐in‐wrap”    “a sign-in wrap lives somewhere in the middle: the website provides a
                   link to terms of use and indicates that some action may bind the user
                   but does not require that the user actually review those terms”

Compare the Second Circuit’s 2017 definitions for the same terms:

      Term                               Second Circuit’s Definition
 “Shrinkwrap”      “a software consumer arguably assents to the license terms contained
                   inside after breaking the shrinkwrap seal and using the enclosed
                   software”
 “Browsewrap”      “generally post terms and conditions on a website via a hyperlink at the
                   bottom of the screen”
 “Clickwrap”       “require users to click an ‘I agree’ box after being presented with a list
                   of terms and conditions of use”
 “Scrollwrap”      “require the user to scroll through the terms before the user can
                   indicate his or her assent by clicking ‘I agree.’”
 “Sign‐in‐wrap”    “notify the user of the existence of the website’s terms of use and,
                   instead of providing an ‘I agree’ button, advise the user that he or she is
                   agreeing to the terms of service when registering or signing up”

Meyer v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017).

If you compare the Chabolla and Meyer definitions, you will notice minor but critical
differences between them. Other courts have adopted yet other definitions of these terms.
In short, semantic confusion over the definitions and meaning of the –wrap taxonomy
regularly causes jurisprudential chaos.

How did we get here? The –wrap terminology dates back to the days when software was
sold in retail stores on physical disks. Manufacturers shipped the disks in individual


                                              68.
cardboard boxes and shrinkwrapped the boxes with plastic. Often, the box would say
something like “by removing the plastic, you are agreeing to software license terms located
inside the box.” (For now, ignore the logic puzzle created by the plastic removal purportedly
binding buyers when they could not actually see the terms until they removed the plastic.
Sometimes the manufacturer avoided this conundrum by printing the terms on the box
itself). Due to the plastic wrapping, these software license agreements became known as
“shrinkwrap” license terms.

As online contracts emerged, lawyers and judges attempted to analogize the user’s
movement around a website to the “unwrapping” of shrinkwrap contracts. See NANCY S.
KIM, WRAP CONTRACTS (2013). This led to the development of the terms “clickwrap” and
“browsewrap.” The “scrollwrap” and “sign-in-wrap” terms came from Berkson v. Gogo LLC,
97 F. Supp. 3d 359 (E.D.N.Y. 2015). Courts have adopted other –wrap terms as well. For
example, several courts have used the term “modified clickwrap” or “hybrid sign-in-wrap.”
One court referenced a “telephone-wrap.”

Unfortunately, the –wrap terminology, though ubiquitous, is frequently problematic.

First, as is often the case, the offline-to-online analogy does not work well. There is a much
greater intentionality and formality to the physical act of removing shrinkwrap plastic
compared to clicking around online.

Second, because of the ill-fitting analogy and constant technological innovations, courts’
definitions of the “wrap” terms have been imprecise. For example, in the Chabolla ruling,
the court defined “clickwrap” as requiring “a popup.” But many formation processes that
require users to make a second click don’t use a popup. So if there’s a second click but no
popup, is it a clickwrap or not? Similarly, a “sign-in-wrap” “does not require that the user
actually review those terms,” but most clickwraps don’t either (though a clickwrap should
force users to review the call-to-action). Thus, if a popup “does not require that the user
actually review those terms,” is it a clickwrap or sign-in-wrap? These kinds of definitional
imprecisions and gaps predictably cause courts to miscategorize the formation process or
proliferate –wrap terms to characterize new facts that don’t clearly fit within the prior
definitions.

Third, the –wrap taxonomy nominally provides a doctrinal tool to bypass the traditional
contract analysis of determining whether each party has sufficiently manifested assent. In
practice, a court’s –wrap analysis often ends up being dicta because the court also conducts
a standard contract assent analysis using standard contract principles, disregarding its –
wrap discussion entirely. See, e.g., Cullinane v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 893 F.3d 53 (1st
Cir. 2018) (“our analysis regarding the existence of an arbitration agreement is not affected
by how we categorize the online contract at issue here.”).

These nomenclature issues may sound academic, but they have had major jurisprudential
and real-world effects. Before the proliferation of –wrap terminology, courts routinely
upheld formation processes where a well-informed user made a single affirmative click.
Now that the –wrap taxonomy distinguishes “clickwraps” (which requires 2 clicks) from
“sign-in-wrap” (which requires only one click), courts will make negative inferences against
businesses that don’t adopt the two-click approach. See, e.g., Cullinane v. Uber
Technologies, Inc., 893 F.3d 53 (1st Cir. 2018) (“Uber chose not to use a common method of


                                              69.
conspicuously informing users of the existence and location of terms and conditions:
requiring users to click a box stating that they agree to a set of terms, often provided by
hyperlink, before continuing to the next screen”); Sarchi v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 268
A.3d 258 (Me. Sup. J. Ct. 2022) (“Uber could have designed its rider app to incorporate
scrollwrap or clickwrap contracts that provided adequate notice of Uber’s original and
updated Terms and required consumers to express actual assent, and it apparently decided
not to do so. The consequence of that choice is that Sarchi was not bound by either the
original Terms or the updated Terms.”).

You can see how the bar got raised in the Chabolla and Godun cases. In the past, courts
likely would have approved both formation processes. Instead, now, as Judge Bybee’s
dissent indicates, the Ninth Circuit’s rulings “drive websites to the only safe harbors
available to them, the clickwrap or scrollwrap agreements.” If you’re wondering why it
seems to take longer to get through the legal boilerplate online, you can thank the courts.

Due to the Chabolla and Godun rulings, you should view pre-2025 TOS formation cases
skeptically, especially “sign-in-wrap” cases. Future courts are likely to be harsher on TOS
formation processes after Chabolla and Godun.

The Black Letter Rules for Browsewraps, Clickwraps, and Scrollwraps

The Chabolla case sets out a spectrum of formation processes. Clickwrap and scrollwrap
processes are the strongest approach to TOS formation and thus are “routinely enforced.”
Browsewraps are the weakest approach to TOS formation, so courts “consistently decline to
enforce browsewraps.”

These sound like black letter rules. If it’s a clickwrap/scrollwrap, it’s enforceable. If it’s a
browsewrap, it’s not.

However…these rules are overshadowed by the inconsistent definitions of the –wrap terms.
Courts routinely misdiagnose the formation process, mislabeling “sign-in-wraps” as
“browsewraps” or “clickwraps.” Thus, cases sometimes enforce browsewraps, such as
Patrick v. Running Warehouse, LLC, 93 F.4th 468 (9th Cir. 2024). In that case, the TOS
formation was clearly a “sign-in-wrap,” not a “browsewrap,” so the ruling upholding the
TOS formation process was consistent with past cases. Nevertheless, the court’s
mislabeling creates a precedent that a “browsewrap” was enforceable, which gives false
hope to defendants and sends confusing signals to other judges.

In other words, the wobbly definitions of various –wrap types ensures jurisprudential
anarchy. The black letter rules are easy to state, but everything goes sideways when courts
or litigators miscategorize the formation process.

Also, although clickwraps/scrollwraps are generally enforceable, these Notes and Questions
will identify specific user interface attributes required for their success. Mismanage those,
and the presumption will evaporate.

“Sign-in-Wraps” Vex the Courts

The Chabolla opinion lays out the black letter rules for “sign-in-wraps”:


                                                70.
       a sign-in wrap agreement may be an enforceable contract based on inquiry
       notice if (1) the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms
       to which the consumer will be bound; and (2) the consumer takes some action,
       such as clicking a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests
       his or her assent to those terms.

The first step, reasonably conspicuous notice, has two subfactors: (A) transaction context,
with the presumption that consumers will expect terms for longer-term transactions but
won’t expect terms for one-off interactions, and (B) the user interface’s visual appearance.

(Note: the courts have manufactured their presumptions about consumers’ contract
expectations for longer-term or one-off interactions. I am not aware of any empirical
evidence validating the courts’ presumptions).

In the Chabolla and Godun cases, the courts reviewed eight different screens and held that
all of them failed to form a contract. Here’s a recap of why each screen failed:

      Screen                                       Why It Failed
 Chabolla Screen 1     Call-to-action wasn’t visually conspicuous because of its “distance
                       from relevant action items, its placement outside of the user’s
                       natural flow, and its font”
 Chabolla Screen 2     No manifestation of assent because call-to-action said “by signing
                       up” and there was no “sign up” button
 Chabolla Screen 3     No manifestation of assent because call-to-action said “I agree to
                       the Terms of Use” and the action button said “Redeem now”
 Godun Screen A        Call-to-action wasn’t visually conspicuous because it was in “small
                       text” and located in “the black background,” which “is outside the
                       main frame of the screen”
 Godun Screen B        Call-to-action wasn’t visually conspicuous (buried grey-on-grey
                       text) and the transaction involves auto-renewals, which require
                       prominent disclosure
 Godun Screen C        Call-to-action wasn’t visually conspicuous because it was not
                       “located directly above or below the action button and is displayed
                       in relatively small text”
 Godun Screens D &     No manifestation of assent because the call-to-action “lacked an
 E                     explanatory phrase” with an if/then grammar

Reminder: because each screen failed individually, the courts refused to combine
disclosures across multiple screens.

Reviewing these explanations of futility is surely frustrating. The businesses could easily
correct all of these issues. For example, if JustAnswers had not prechecked the boxes in
Screens D & E and instead required users to affirmatively check those boxes, the screens
would have been clickwraps and presumptively properly formed. Still, these businesses
might have (over-optimistically) assumed their formation approaches satisfied the then-
prevailing legal standards, only to receive a harsh wakeup call at the Ninth Circuit.




                                              71.
While businesses can and should avoid the traps identified in the Chabolla and Godun
opinions, the judges in those opinions applied exacting standards to their reviews of the
user interfaces. As Judge Nelson self-concurred, these opinions “demand magic words”—
which perhaps prioritizes form over substance. For example, if the users understood what “I
agree” means in context, does it really matter if the formation process used an if/then
grammar? The Chabolla and Godun courts embraced a degree of heightened contract
formalism compared to most appellate rulings preceding them. And it’s not clear other
circuits will follow. See Dhruva v. CuriosityStream, Inc., 131 F.4th 146 (4th Cir. 2025) (the
court excused a call-to-action that said “you agree that you’ve read our Terms of Use and
Privacy Policy,” even though the call-to-action didn’t say that users actually agree to the
TOU).

Test Yourself: Do users in fact agree to the T&Cs in this user interface?




See TopstepTrader, LLC, V. OneUp Trader, LLC, 2018 WL 1859040 (N.D. Ill. 2018) (no,
because “the ‘Sign Up’ button signaled that the user wanted to sign up for an account; it did
not signal acceptance to additional Terms”).




                                             72.
Test Yourself: Do users agree to the TOU by clicking the “pay now” button?




See Ghazizadeh v. Coursera, Inc., 737 F. Supp. 3d 911 (N.D. Cal. 2024) (no, because
Coursera never tells consumers that “pay now” button signals the consumers’ assent to the
“I agree to the Terms of Use” statement).

Following Chabolla and Godun, the Ninth Circuit would say that both of the preceding
screenshots also fail to form the terms because the “I agree to” call-to-action is missing the
“if” part of the if/then grammar.

How Should Online Businesses Properly Form Their TOSes?

In dissent, Judge Bybee said:

       The result is one of caveat websitus internetus (roughly translated as
       “internet websites beware!”). Our decision today will drive websites to the
       only safe harbors available to them, the clickwrap or scrollwrap agreements.

This warning deserves heeding. Even though it’s possible to form online TOSes
using a one-click formation process, a properly implemented two-click process acts
like a “safe harbor.” The first click should be a checkbox saying something like “by



                                              73.
checking the box on the left, you agree to the terms and conditions.” The second click
should advance the user to the next stage in the process (i.e., it’s an action button).

If a business decides to rely on a single-click formation process despite the courts’
warnings, the business should shout, not whisper, its call-to-action. There should not
be any mystery or subtlety in how the call-to-action is displayed. Thus, as the
Chabolla case indicated, the TOS call-to-action shouldn’t use “timid” font sizes or
colors; the call-to-action should be located within the “user’s natural flow”; the call-
to-action should not be displayed amidst “muddled” transitions; and the call-to-
action should use an if/then grammar; and the language in the “if” component
should precisely match the action button’s label. If this sounds like a lot of work and
risk, then it’s a reminder of why many businesses will prefer the legal safe harbor of
a two-click process.

How to Display Hyperlinked Terms. If courts are going to scrutinize user interfaces with
huge skepticism, then every design choice matters—all the way down to how the call-to-
action displays any links to the TOS. (This issue can be avoided by displaying the full TOS
terms on the same page as the formation process, but many services find this approach too
cluttered or distracting).

From a legal standpoint, the safest choice is to link to the TOS using a blue underlined font.
However, other colors might be OK. For example, Airbnb put its hyperlinks in red. When a
user argued that he didn’t expect red hyperlinks, the DC Circuit replied: “Reasonable notice
does not turn on where the hyperlinked text falls on the color wheel; rather we consider
whether the text was conspicuous.” Selden v. Airbnb, Inc., 4 F.4th 148 (D.C. Cir. 2021).

However, the absence of underlining may be fatal to formation. See Berman v. Freedom
Financial Network, LLC, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022); In re StubHub Refund Litigation,
2023 WL 5092759 (9th Cir. 2023) (non-underlined gray text wasn’t prominent enough, plus
the court was distracted by a hot pink action button); Tejon v. Zeus Networks LLC, 725 F.
Supp. 3d 1351 (S.D. Fla. 2024).

Test Yourself: Expedia presented its TOU and privacy policy this way:




Does the infinity-like symbol adequately convey the link to the TOU and privacy policy?
Beland v. Expedia, Inc., 2021 WL 3046742 (Cal. App. Ct. 2021) (yes, when the plaintiffs
admitted that they knew the symbol signified a hyperlink—but please never use symbols
like this).

Avoiding the Need to Authenticate Users. When an online TOS formation process is properly
executed, the online service doesn’t need to prove the identity of each individual user who
purportedly agreed to it. Instead, the service can demonstrate that all of its users navigated
through the same userflow that included a page where contract formation was done right.



                                              74.
Thus, it should be impossible for users to reach their desired outcome (such as creating the
account or buying the item) without going through the TOS formation process.

To uphold this premise, users should not be able to reach the end destination in other way.
If they can get to the end without going through the TOS formation, then the process has
“leaks” that jeopardize TOS formation for all users. See Snyder v. G6 Hospitality LLC, 2025
WL 1254382 (C.D. Cal. 2025) (“Regardless of whether the website’s sign-up page that
Defendant cites may have provided Plaintiff constructive notice, Defendant has not
established by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff signed up using that method,
as opposed to using either of the two sign-up pages which provided no notice.”).

Instead of requiring users to create a new account, many services give users the option to
log in using third-party services such as Google or Facebook (the “OAuth” protocol). If a
user chooses this option, the user will usually click on a link that takes them away from the
service’s TOS formation process. In other words, a “Log In With Facebook” option becomes a
potential “leak” in the TOS formation process. A lawyer must carefully review each and
every link on the TOS formation page to ensure that the formation process isn’t leaky. See
Lee v. Plex, Inc., 773 F. Supp. 3d 755 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (an option to “sign up with Facebook”
undermined TOS formation).

TOS Formation and Children. Even if a business uses a perfectly implemented clickwrap, it
still runs into formation problems with any users who have a legally recognized limitation
to forming binding contracts, such as intoxication, mental incapacity, or status as a minor.
Even though the formation process operated properly from a technical and logical
standpoint, the consumer’s lack of capacity could undermine the contract’s validity.

C.M.D. v. Facebook, Inc., 2014 WL 1266291 (N.D. Cal. 2014), dealt with Facebook’s use of
minors’ names and faces in on-site advertising. Facebook claimed the minors agreed to
Facebook’s advertising practices via its TOS (what Facebook calls its “Statement of Rights
and Responsibilities”). The court held that, according to the applicable California statute,
the agreement was voidable, not void ab initio. Minors could choose to void the contract at
any time, but only by terminating their Facebook accounts. Until the minors made this
election, the contract was legally valid. Thus, Facebook wasn’t liable for its advertising
practices prior to voiding.

In B.F. v. Amazon.com, Inc., 2019 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 230144 (W.D. Wash. 2019), the court
held that Amazon Alexa’s TOS did not bind children, even if their parents had consented to
the TOS. However, Amazon could have added a provision to its TOS saying that parents
were consenting on behalf of their children.

In a lawsuit against Roblox, the plaintiff alleged that a majority of its users are under 13. A
court said that, with respect to the screenshot below, the TOU never formed: “Even if the
notice would be sufficiently conspicuous and understandable for an adult, it is not for a
child….A child—even a reasonably prudent one—would not be on inquiry notice that she
was assenting to an agreement from this set of facts.” Doe v. Roblox Corp., 602 F. Supp. 3d
1243 (N.D. Cal. 2022).




                                              75.
How should businesses deal with the inevitability that some minors will be in the
population of users who nominally agree to its TOS?

As the Child Safety chapter explores, governments are increasingly requiring online
services to determine the ages of their users and then restrict minors’ access to those
services. If a service authenticates a user as a minor but doesn’t block them from forming
the TOS (for example, if the law requires blocking under-16s, but the age of majority is 18),
what happens next? Will the potential risk of TOS formation failure give businesses
another reason to close their doors to all minors?

Uber’s TOS Formation Madness. An entire chapter could be dedicated solely to drama
associated with Uber’s TOS!

Mobile Device Madness: To register and create an account with Uber, customers had to
navigate the following process. First, they completed this screen:




                                             76.
77.
After clicking “next,” registrants saw the following screen:




In 2017, in Meyer v. Uber, the Second Circuit blessed this TOS formation interface. (Would
the Ninth Circuit approve it now?) However, when registrants attempted to enter their


                                              78.
credit card data (which they had to do to finish the registration process), the above screen
changed to look like this:




Notice how once the user starts to enter the credit card number, the keypad covers up the
language “By creating an Uber account, you agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy
Policy,” but the “Register” button remains visible. As a result, registrants who filled in their
credit card information and immediately selected the “Register” button would not see the
“By creating an Uber account…” language again.


                                              79.
Does this user interface jeopardize Uber’s contract formation? Metter v. Uber Techs., Inc.,
2017 WL 1374579 (N.D. Cal. 2017), contains this ominous statement: “Although the terms
of service alert seems designed to put a registrant on inquiry notice of Uber’s terms of
service and to alert the registrant that registration will amount to affirmative assent to
those terms, the keypad obstruction is a fatal defect to the alert’s functioning.”

Imagine you are counsel for Uber when it rolled out the implementation described above.
Would you have structured the user interface differently? If so, ask yourself how you would
have spotted this issue. If mobile device apps function differently, sometimes substantially,
depending on the operating system (i.e., Apple v. Android), what steps would you take to
properly review Uber’s contract formation in its apps?

Massachusetts Madness: In Kauders v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 486 Mass. 557 (2021), the
Massachusetts Supreme Court declared that Uber’s TOS failed for Massachusetts
consumers. The court said that Uber didn’t provide reasonable notice to consumers because:

       the interface did not require the user to scroll through the conditions or even
       select them. The user could fully register for the service and click “done”
       without ever clicking the link to the terms and conditions. The connection
       between the creation of the account and the terms and conditions was also
       somewhat oddly displayed in the two-part format, with the significant
       information (i.e., that by creating the account, the user expresses his or her
       agreement) being displayed less prominently than other information….

       Nothing about [Uber’s registration screen] conveyed to a user that he or she
       should open a link that would reveal an extensive set of terms and conditions
       at the bottom of the screen to which the user was agreeing….the statement
       explaining the connection between creating the account and agreeing to the
       terms, which would encourage opening and reviewing the terms, was
       displayed less prominently than the other information on the screen.

       Similarly, the title of the screen, as well as much of the information on the
       screen, focused on payment information, not the terms and conditions. Other
       words on the screen also appeared as prominently as the link, if not more
       so….

       a user could complete the “LINK PAYMENT” screen and the account creation
       process without ever focusing on the link or the notice on the screen. [the
       court also noted how the credit card input fields could hide the call-to-action,
       as just discussed above]…

       the final step in the process was to input payment information and click
       “DONE.” “DONE” is also different from, and less clear than, other affirmative
       language such as “I agree.” Furthermore, there was nothing stating that
       “DONE” itself signified either creation of an account or acceptance of
       the terms.




                                              80.
See also Sarchi v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 268 A.3d 258 (Me. Sup. J. Ct. 2022) (agreeing
with Kauders, the court says Uber’s “DONE” button didn’t tell consumers they were also
agreeing to the terms).

Kauders was obviously a disappointing ruling for Uber, because other courts had blessed
similar or identical TOS presentations. After that ruling, can you imagine the panic and
turmoil among Uber’s legal department? The Massachusetts Supreme Court had just said
that Uber had no contracts with any Massachusetts users, and that left Uber highly
exposed to lawsuits.

In response, Uber required all Massachusetts users to click through the following screen:




                                             81.
The screen’s headline, “We’ve updated our terms,” is an interesting wording choice because,
according to Kauders, Uber didn’t have any TOS in place with Massachusetts users that it
could “update.” Do you think this TOS presentation solved the problems raised by the
Kauders court sufficient to be properly formed? See Good v. Uber Technologies, Inc., 494
Mass. 116 (2024) (court said it worked! And Uber breathed a huge sigh of relief); Wu v.
Uber Technologies, Inc., 43 N.Y.3d 288 (N.Y. Ct. App. 2024) (the update also worked in New
York!). Even so, could you improve this screen?

Uber’s Massachusetts Madness is a good cautionary reminder for every business. You
NEVER want a court striking down your TOS. The liability exposure will be enormous and
fixing the problem will be a time-consuming and costly process.

Because of the stakes of properly executing the contract formation process, the lawyer’s
responsibility isn’t just to draft and deliver the substantive legal terms. The lawyer must
then guide and confirm the contract formation implementation to ensure it’s airtight. This
includes investigating possible leaks and checking the formation on multiple devices and
operating systems. Mobile apps intrinsically require a different sequence of steps than
websites, and if either sequence fails to form the contract, the service’s TOS formation is in
trouble. Further, app implementations often differ between iOS, Android, and other mobile
device operating systems (and the sequences may differ between different versions of each
operating system). IT IS THE LAWYER’S JOB TO CONFIRM THE CONTRACT
FORMATION PROCESS WORKS AS EXPECTED ACROSS ALL OF THE DIFFERENT
MODALITIES. LAWYERS SHOULD NEVER ASSUME THE CLIENT WILL GET THIS
RIGHT ON ITS OWN.

Does Time Pressure Matter? In the Uber cases, some plaintiffs argued that they didn’t have
a lot of time to review the TOS formation request because they were rushing to get to their
destination. In theory, time pressure could contribute to a finding of procedural
unconscionability, but does it negate TOS formation?

In Washington v. Flixbus, Inc., 2025 WL 1592961 (S.D. Cal. 2025), the plaintiffs were
booking bus tickets. The system put their ticket reservations on hold for 10 minutes so that
the plaintiffs could complete the purchase, including agreeing to the TOS. The plaintiffs
claimed that the 10 minute window wasn’t sufficient time to review the TOS terms. The
court responded:

       The Court rejects Plaintiff’s contention that users “do not assent” to
       Defendant’s terms because a user with an average reading speed cannot
       finish reading the Privacy Policy and Terms and Conditions before the
       checkout timer elapses. It similarly rejects Plaintiff’s suggestion that the
       countdown timer imposes undue pressure that negates any consent users do
       provide via the checkbox. If a user has not completed reviewing Defendant’s
       terms before ten minutes have elapsed, the user is under no obligation to
       complete the checkout process. This remains the case even it this means the
       user’s selected seats may no longer be available after the timer elapses.
       Further, as Defendant notes and Plaintiff acknowledges in his opposition, if
       users wish to review Defendant’s Privacy Policy and Terms and Conditions
       outside the checkout process, they may access the policies at any time via
       hyperlinks at the bottom of Defendant’s website.


                                              82.
The Restatements §69 Workaround. From Register.com, Inc. v. Verio, Inc., 356 F.3d 393 (2d
Cir. 2004):

       We recognize that contract offers on the Internet often require the offeree to
       click on an “I agree” icon. And no doubt, in many circumstances, such a
       statement of agreement by the offeree is essential to the formation of a
       contract. But not in all circumstances. While new commerce on the Internet
       has exposed courts to many new situations, it has not fundamentally changed
       the principles of contract. It is standard contract doctrine that when a benefit
       is offered subject to stated conditions, and the offeree makes a decision to
       take the benefit with knowledge of the terms of the offer, the taking
       constitutes an acceptance of the terms, which accordingly become binding on
       the offeree. See, e.g., Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 69(1)(a) (1981)
       (“[S]ilence and inaction operate as an acceptance ... [w]here an offeree takes
       the benefit of offered services with reasonable opportunity to reject them and
       reason to know that they were offered with the expectation of
       compensation.”); 2 Richard A. Lord, Williston on Contracts § 6:9 (4th ed.
       1991) (“[T]he acceptance of the benefit of services may well be held to imply a
       promise to pay for them if at the time of acceptance the offeree has a
       reasonable opportunity to reject the service and knows or has reason to know
       that compensation is expected.”); Arthur Linton Corbin, Corbin on Contracts
       § 71 (West 1 vol. ed. 1952) (“The acceptance of the benefit of the services is a
       promise to pay for them, if at the time of accepting the benefit the offeree has
       a reasonable opportunity to reject it and knows that compensation is
       expected.”); Jones v. Brisbin, 41 Wash. 2d 167, 172 (1952) (“Where a person,
       with reasonable opportunity to reject offered services, takes the benefit of
       them under circumstances which would indicate, to a reasonable man, that
       they were offered with the expectation of compensation, a contract, complete
       with mutual assent, results.”); Markstein Bros. Millinery Co. v. J.A. White &
       Co., 151 Ark. 1 (1921) (buyer of hats was bound to pay for hats when buyer
       failed to return them to seller within five days of inspection as seller
       requested in clear and obvious notice statement).

Restatements §69 addressed a specific business practice called “standing orders,” i.e., a
vendor places an open-ended order to accept a supplier’s goods when shipped to the vendor,
subject to the vendor’s right to reject or return the items if the vendor doesn’t approve of the
goods. With standing orders, if the vendor keeps the goods, the vendor has to pay the
supplier’s price. In other words, a standing order defines the parties’ relationship in
advance, with each delivery constituting its own standalone contract for those items. You
can occasionally find standing orders in the field today, but they are largely a relic of the
past.

Some courts have transformed the Restatements §69 principle into a more generalized rule
that an entity is bound by contract when they take a benefit knowing of the terms attached
to the benefit. Restating the rule at this level of abstraction strips away the standing order
context. Instead, the rule potentially becomes a general-purpose workaround to standard
contract principles about manifestations of assent.



                                              83.
Accordingly, this workaround threatens to swallow up all of contract law. Recall what the
Register.com court said: “in many circumstances, such a statement of agreement by the
offeree is essential to the formation of a contract. But not in all circumstances.” In those
other circumstances, the court is waiving the requirement that both parties affirmatively
manifest assent to the terms. This would make it too easy for a business to impose
unwanted terms on non-consenting users. Courts are reluctant to do that.

In the Internet context, courts theoretically could use the Restatements §69 principle to
find a contract where a business has posted a TOS but the users didn’t affirmatively
manifest assent to it through an appropriately executed –wrap. In those circumstances,
courts say that the users would still be bound to the terms if they knew of the terms and
still “took the benefits.”

This principle can come into play when automated agents interact with a website, such as
spammers who send emails to an email server or robots/scrapers collect information from a
website. The Restatements §69 principle would say that the spammers or scrapers are
bound by the TOS terms (such as a contractual restriction on spamming or scraping) if the
spammer/scraper knew of the TOS but sent the automated agents anyway.

That’s what the Register.com v. Verio opinion held in a scraping case. The court explained:

       Verio’s argument might well be persuasive if its queries addressed to
       Register’s computers had been sporadic and infrequent. If Verio had
       submitted only one query, or even if it had submitted only a few sporadic
       queries, that would give considerable force to its contention that it obtained
       the WHOIS data without being conscious that Register intended to impose
       conditions, and without being deemed to have accepted Register’s conditions.
       But Verio was daily submitting numerous queries, each of which resulted in
       its receiving notice of the terms Register exacted. Furthermore, Verio admits
       that it knew perfectly well what terms Register demanded.

(Importantly, the defendant Verio conceded that it had knowledge of Register.com’s terms,
which sidestepped an analytically difficult issue—when do automated agents “know”
anything?).

In contrast, the Chabolla and Godun opinions indicate how courts will increasingly reject
TOS formation when businesses don’t use properly executed –wraps. Given that
intolerance, the Restatements §69 workaround and its disregard for affirmative
manifestations of assent seems even more problematic. Businesses can always try
Restatements §69 as a last-ditch argument if their TOS formation fails, but those
arguments should rarely succeed.

Post-Transaction Emails. Sometimes, businesses try to form their TOSes via email
communications after consumers have already made their purchases or created their
accounts. This is a pretty sketchy practice, and it’s not likely to lead to TOS formation.

For example, Trilegiant sent emails containing the legal terms after users enrolled in its
subscription services. The Second Circuit said the post-enrollment emails didn’t create
inquiry notice:


                                              84.
       the plaintiffs were presented with the arbitration provision in an email
       delivered to each of them after they had enrolled in Great Fun. Trilegiant
       asserts that the fact that we can assume that the email was received by the
       plaintiffs is enough to support the conclusion that they were on inquiry notice
       of its terms. But that someone has received an email does not without more
       establish that he or she should know that the terms disclosed in the email
       relate to a service in which he or she had previously enrolled and that a
       failure affirmatively to opt out of the service amounts to assent to those
       terms....

       the arbitration provision here was both temporally and spatially decoupled
       from the plaintiffs’ enrollment in and use of Great Fun; the term was
       delivered after initial enrollment and Great Fun members such as the
       plaintiffs would not be forced to confront the terms while enrolling in or using
       the service or maintaining their memberships....

       a reasonable person would not be expected to connect an email that the
       recipient may not actually see until long after enrolling in a service (if ever)
       with the contractual relationship he or she may have with the service
       provider, especially where the enrollment required as little effort as it did for
       the plaintiffs here.

Schnabel v. Trilegiant, 697 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. 2012); see also Starke v. SquareTrade, Inc.,
913 F.3d 279 (2d Cir. 2019); Seneca v. Homeaglow, Inc., 2025 WL 852896 (9th Cir. 2025)
(web screen presenting TOS formation came too late because the consumer had already
made the purchase); but compare Sadlock v. Walt Disney Corp., 2023 WL 4869245 (N.D.
Cal. 2023) (“emails followed by continued use is sufficient to establish assent”).

We’ll revisit TOS formation by email when we discuss post-formation TOS amendments
communicated by email.

Evidentiary Issues. Assume an online service has a well-drafted TOS and a well-executed
TOS formation process. How can the online service credibly prove its contract formation
process and applicable terms in court…preferably at the motion to dismiss stage?

In Moretti v. Hertz Corporation, 2014 WL 1410432 (N.D. Cal. 2014), Hotwire invoked its
TOU against a plaintiff who claimed he hadn’t checked the box to assent to the agreement.
To support a motion to transfer, Hotwire introduced the following evidence:

       Defendants have produced two declarations from employees at Hotwire: (1)
       Sarah Bernard who at the operative time was the Vice President of Product
       Management for Hotwire; and (2) Jacob Aaron Joachin Hadary who was the
       Lead Product Manager for Hotwire during that time. Bernard and Hadary
       affirmatively state that the Terms of Use in operation during the December
       2012 time frame included a forum-selection clause. Hadary declares, and
       corroborates Bernard’s declaration, that an individual using the Hotwire
       website cannot complete a booking without checking the “Acceptance Box”
       acknowledging the acceptance of “Hotwire’s terms and conditions and other


                                              85.
       applicable rules.” Hadary confirms that this requirement has been in place
       since 2005.

Based on those declarations, and without any conflicting evidence from the plaintiff
other than an unsubstantiated assertion, the court upheld Hotwire’s venue-selection
clause and granted its motion to transfer.

In Zaltz v. JDate, 952 F. Supp. 2d 439 (E.D.N.Y. 2013), JDate used a two-click process for
registration. First, users must check-the-box to confirm reading the terms, then click on a
button to confirm registration. Nevertheless, the plaintiff claimed: “I don’t believe these are
the same terms I signed up with. I don’t believe that I agreed to any terms stating that I
have to sue within California if an issue arises.” JDate rebutted her unsupported assertion
with screenshots of its registration page plus:

       a sworn statement from its North American Director of Customer Support
       that the “Terms of Service were applicable to all subscribers of Spark
       Networks’ website at JDate.com and no material changes were made thereto
       during all four periods where Ms. Zaltz was a subscriber of Spark’s website at
       JDate.com” and the forum selection clause at issue was part of those Terms of
       Service and “remained unchanged during Ms. Zaltz’s subscription to
       JDate.com.”

On this basis, JDate successfully transferred the case to its home court without a mini-trial
to resolve what contract terms governed the case.

To achieve similar results, it’s essential to maintain a chain of evidence that can
convincingly show (1) the agreement’s terms on any specific date, and (2) what user
interactions were technologically required to manifest assent on that date (preferably
including screenshots in color or a video if the formation page has any kinetic elements).
The chain of evidence should have enough integrity that it can be introduced even if all of
the relevant employees have left the company by the time the matter reaches litigation. For
examples of how evidentiary issues can foil contract enforceability, see Snow v. Eventbrite,
Inc., 2020 WL 6135990 (N.D. Cal. 2020); Sellers v. Bleacher Report, Inc., 2023 WL 4850180
(N.D. Cal. 2023).

Note: you can typically find old versions of TOSes at the Internet Archive’s Wayback
Machine, but watch out! Those archival copies may be missing important pieces of the user
interface, especially any animation, and the Wayback Machine may not capture the exact
date of any changes. You should never rely on the Wayback Machine as your primary
source of archival copies of a business’ TOS; the Wayback Machine is the last-ditch option
when you have nothing else.

The Swinging Pendulum of Arbitration Enforceability. This chapter primarily focuses on
the procedure of online contract formation, not the substantive terms of the contract. If the
formation process is botched, the substantive contract terms don’t matter. See Doe v. Roblox
Corp., 602 F. Supp. 3d 1243 (N.D. Cal. 2022). But if contract formation is handled properly,
then the substantive terms of that contract absolutely matter—especially when challenged
as unconscionable.



                                              86.
The Federal Arbitration Act says that agreements to arbitrate generally shall be “valid,
irrevocable, and enforceable.” 9 U.S.C. §2. Accordingly, courts often go to great lengths to
honor arbitration agreements. Some of this reflects courts’ workloads—every case sent to
arbitration shrinks the judge’s docket. More importantly, arbitration has the reputation of
being cheaper and faster than litigation, so getting cases into arbitration theoretically
benefits everyone.

This pro-arbitration view has degraded in the last couple decades. First, arbitration often
isn’t faster or cheaper than litigation. Second, businesses stack the deck by selecting
arbitration services where they are likely to win consistently. If a business doesn’t like the
outcomes or the rules, it will switch arbitration services. See Brooks v. WarnerMedia
Direct, LLC, 2024 WL 3330305 (S.D.N.Y. 2024). Third, arbitrations bypass jury trials (and
the associated risk of high damage awards from those trials) and sometimes inhibit the
formation of class actions, helping businesses skirt important consumer protective
doctrines.

As courts recognized the potential abuses of arbitration clauses, they became more
circumspect about sending cases to arbitration. For example, in Comb v. PayPal, 218 F.
Supp. 2d 1165 (2002), a federal court deemed PayPal’s arbitration clause unconscionable.
Following the Comb decision, many online businesses removed arbitration clauses from
their online contracts.

The pendulum swung back after AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion, 563 U.S. 333 (2011), which
invalidated states’ efforts to restrict arbitration, even when arbitration blocked class action
lawsuits. Following Concepcion, many online businesses added arbitration clauses into
their online contracts. However, most businesses now take several steps to reduce the risk
of the clause being unconscionable, such as excluding low-value cases (letting those go to
small claims court), allowing class formation in arbitration, covering the out-of-pocket costs
for the arbitration service, allowing consumers to arbitrate without making a costly
appearance in person, and letting consumers opt-out of arbitration when forming the
contract (usually via an onerous opt-out mechanism, such as sending a postal letter within
30 days of agreeing to the terms).

Plaintiffs are making countermoves of their own. In particular, if a business offers to cover
the arbitration costs (which the business does to reduce the risk that the arbitration clause
is unconscionable), plaintiffs can file thousands of arbitration requests (a process called
“mass arbitration”) as a way of draining the business’ litigation budget before the cases
even get started. For example, when 5,000 Doordash workers initiated arbitration instead
of a class action lawsuit, Doordash faced about $10M in upfront arbitration filing fees.
Abernathy v. Doordash, Inc., 438 F. Supp. 3d 1062 (N.D. Cal. 2020). As a result, some
businesses are now once again removing arbitration clauses from their TOSes. See Sara
Randazzo, Amazon Faced 75,000 Arbitration Demands. Now It Says: Fine, Sue Us, WALL
ST. J., June 1, 2021; Michael Corkery, Amazon Ends Use of Arbitration for Customer
Disputes, N.Y. TIMES, July 22, 2021, https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/22/business/amazon-
arbitration-customer-disputes.html.

If you’re advising a business about online contract formation that includes an arbitration
clause, make sure to keep up with the caselaw and the state-of-the-art arbitration terms
that reduce the risk of unconscionability. The law in this area changes rapidly.
