                                                         ***

The Internet is an electronic network, but all Internet packets move over physical-space
“chattels” such as routers, servers, and data lines. Someone, usually a private entity, owns
that chattel. The “trespass to chattels” doctrines determine when those property owners can
exclude others from using their property.

Before defining trespass to chattels, it’s helpful to review three related legal concepts.

Trespass to real property restricts unconsented presence on someone’s land. Typically, a
landowner enjoin trespassers without showing the landowner suffered any legally
recognizable damage from a past trespass. In other words, the unauthorized physical
presence of a person on someone else’s land is enough to support a claim. Trespass to real
property doesn’t have any meaningful relationship to Internet Law. Every chattel
associated with the Internet resides on someone’s real property, but misuse of that chattel
isn’t considered a trespass to the land where the chattel is located.




                                                          105.
Nuisance is a non-possessory interference with someone’s enjoyment of their real property,
such as when a neighbor’s activities generates odors or smoke particulates that drift onto
someone else’s land and diminish their enjoyment. Internet activities aren’t a legal
“nuisance,” even when they have real effects on real property. See In re Social Media Cases,
JCCP 5255 (Cal. Superior Ct. June 7, 2024) (“The School District cannot elide the principles
of foreseeability, duty, zone of risk, and proximate cause that govern the outcome of a
common law claim of negligence by substituting an assertion that the outcome of [the social
media defendants’] conduct has been a nuisance”); but compare Commonwealth v. Meta
Platforms, Inc., 2024 Mass. Super. LEXIS 161 (Mass. Superior Ct. Oct. 17, 2024) (“the
Commonwealth alleges that Meta has contributed to a youth mental health crisis by
promoting the addictive use of its platform. This is sufficient to support a public nuisance
claim”).

Conversion (or “theft”) is the permanent deprivation of someone’s chattel. It is both a tort
and a crime. Although conversion generally applies only to tangible personal property, it
occasionally shows up in Internet Law with respect to “thefts” of intangible personal
property, such as domain name registrations. See Kremen v. Cohen, 337 F.3d 1024 (2003);
see also Taylor v. Google LLC, 2024 WL 837044 (9th Cir. 2024) (cellular data is capable of
being converted). Be careful applying conversion law to the Internet, however. Many
activities online don’t reach the level of conversion; and copyright law preempts any use of
the conversion doctrine to cover assets that copyright law regulates or deregulates. As a
result, Internet Law-related conversion claims often fail. E.g., Best Carpet Values, Inc. v.
Google LLC, 90 F.4th 962 (9th Cir. 2024) (web page framing isn’t conversion); Edible IP,
LLC v. Google, LLC, 313 Ga. 305 (Ga. 2022) (competitive keyword advertising isn’t
conversion).

Trespass to chattels is sometimes described as the little sibling of conversion. Trespass to
chattels applies to non-permanent interferences with someone’s chattel. (A permanent
interference would be conversion). For example, an old time trespass to chattels was taking
someone’s vehicle (the chattel) for a “joyride.” If the interloper intends to keep the vehicle
permanently, that may be conversion/theft. Otherwise, if the interloper returns the vehicle,
then it may be a trespass to chattels. Though the doctrine of trespass to chattels is a very
old common law doctrine, it’s rarely litigated today outside of the Internet context because
the enforcement costs overwhelm any potential damages.

In contrast, the trespass to chattels doctrine has potentially existential implications for the
Internet. If a chattel owner connected to the Internet can require third parties to obtain
permission to use it, then the chattel owner can establish tollbooths to access its chattel and
charge for or block usage of their chattel. Collectively, those tollbooths create a rights
thicket for everyone trying to communicate on the Internet—each message exchange would
need to negotiate every tollbooth, and the time and cost of doing so would make it
impossible to accomplish even the simplest online task.

Instead, the law normally assumes that if someone connects their chattel to the Internet,
they anticipate and impliedly consent to normal Internet usage (otherwise, the owners can
disconnect the chattel from the Internet).




                                             106.
At the same time, if a chattel owner can’t exclude users from its chattel, malefactors can
overgraze the chattel and crowd out all legitimate uses. Establishing a balance between
permitting legitimate and blocking illegitimate chattel usage has vexed Internet Law for
decades.

As indicated by the chart above, there are three main overlapping Internet trespass to
chattels (TTC) doctrines:

      Common law trespass to chattels applies to the unconsented use of someone’s
       Internet-connected chattel that causes legally recognizable harm. This doctrine
       doesn’t get litigated very often, but any case addressing it typically raises important
       policy issues.
      The Computer Fraud & Abuse Act (CFAA, 18 U.S.C. § 1030). Congress enacted the
       CFAA in the 1980s to restrict certain computer crimes. It has been amended many
       times over the years and, in addition to its criminal provisions, provides a federal
       civil claim that covers a lot of the same territory as the common law trespass to
       chattels doctrine. The CFAA’s statutory drafting is terrible, so it’s an extremely
       difficult statute to read and interpret. As the chart above shows, several subsections
       are potentially relevant, each with their own detailed requirements. Overall, the
       most commonly litigated provision in civil cases is 1030(a)(5), which itself has
       subsections with their own requirements.
      State computer crime laws, such as California Penal Code § 502. Some of these laws
       date back to the 1970s, so they have antiquated terms and assumptions. Often, the
       laws contain a laundry list of overlapping and confusingly worded restrictions. Like
       the CFAA, these laws may also provide civil remedies.

Depending on the defendant’s activity, other potentially related legal doctrines include
breach of contract and copyright law.

Most TTC lawsuits turn on two main issues:

      Was the defendant’s use of the chattel “unauthorized,” and how did the defendant
       know that? If we assume that every chattel owner who connects to the Internet
       impliedly permits some usage, then the chattel owner has the de facto burden to
       remove that implied permission—by delimiting their chattel’s usage and effectively
       communicating those limits to defendants. This is more complicated than it sounds.
       For example, you might assume that a contract with the defendant would ensure
       that the chattel owner properly communicated those limits to the defendant, but
       counterintuitively that issue remains legally unsettled.
      Did the defendant’s usage cause sufficient legally recognizable harm? Even if the
       defendant made unexpected or unpermitted usage of the chattel, it may only cause
       de minimis harms or harms the laws aren’t designed to prevent. For example, many
       CFAA cases require that the defendant caused $5,000 or more of legally recognized
       harms. If the defendant caused harm below that threshold, the CFAA claim may
       fail.




                                             107.
As you have already inferred, this area of the law is chaotic. There are three overlapping
doctrines with several others in play, poorly drafted statutes, and high policy stakes.
Typically, TTC cases raise more questions than they answer.

                                                       ***

Trespass to chattels issues pop up all over Internet Law, including departing employees
who take electronic files, advertising and privacy (such as the placement of cookies on a
user’s device—see Doe v. Tenet Healthcare Corp., 2025 WL 1635956 (E.D. Cal. 2025)), and
spam (when spammers send bulk email to a third-party email server). This section will
focus on “scraping,” the process of using automated tools to gather data from third-party
services.

The following case involves Bright Data, a company that scrapes data from Twitter* to
build a marketing database. Bright Data makes automated requests of Twitter’s servers
and collects data from the pages delivered by Twitter. Twitter doesn’t inherently object to
people making requests of its servers; its customers necessarily do that to use the service.
Twitter also doesn’t object to bulk data accesses of the content on its servers, but only if the
data collectors use its “API” that makes it efficient for Twitter to deliver data in bulk.
Twitter charges a lot of money for API access; and Bright Data either didn’t want to pay or
didn’t qualify for access per the API rules.

Much of the value in Twitter’s database is third-party content uploaded from its users,
which Twitter doesn’t own. Instead, its users have copyright and privacy interests in their
tweets that the user can’t easily enforce directly against Bright Data. Thus, either Twitter
brings an enforcement action on their behalf, or Bright Data may get away with violating
the tweeters’ rights. But when Twitter brings an anti-scraping enforcement action, it’s
probably not representing its users’ interests. For example, as the court in the next case
says, “X Corp…is not looking to protect X users’ privacy.” Instead, X wants Bright Data to
pay for API access or wants to cut Bright Data off entirely. (In the opinion below, the court
says “X Corp. is happy to allow the extraction and copying of X users’ content so long as it
gets paid.”). In particular, Twitter might want to offer services that compete with Bright
Data, which raises a competition law angle to Twitter’s enforcement action

As you can see, Twitter’s anti-scraping enforcement action against Bright Data raises
numerous policy considerations. To succeed in court, Twitter must fit its objections into the
specific legal doctrines or a court won’t recognize them. Let’s take a look at how a court
handled Twitter’s concerns.

X Corp. v. Bright Data Ltd., 733 F. Supp. 3d 832 (N.D. Cal. 2024)

…Those who register for accounts on X can post comments, images, and videos, as well as
interact with others who have registered for accounts on X by re-posting, liking, and
commenting on their posts. Those who do not register for accounts on X can still access the
platform, however. According to X Corp., “[a]ll users who register for a X account, and/or
view the X website or application agree to a binding contract with X Corp. as outlined in X


* [“X” is the confusing rebrand of the former “Twitter” service.]




                                                        108.
Corp.’s User Agreement, which is comprised of the Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, and the
Rules and Policies (collectively the ‘Terms’).”

1. Pertinent Provisions….
the Terms restrict many forms of “Misuse of the Services.” These restrictions are the
fulcrum of the instant complaint. Relevant here, the Terms provide that “[i]f you want to
reproduce, modify, create derivative works, distribute, sell, transfer, publicly display,
publicly perform, transmit, or otherwise use the Services or Content on the Services, you
must use the interfaces and instructions we provide, except as permitted through the
Services, these Terms, or the [developer] terms .... Otherwise, all such actions are strictly
prohibited.” Separately, the Terms ban an X user from scraping, unambiguously stating
that “scraping the Services in any form, for any purpose without our prior written consent
is expressly prohibited.”

As our court of appeals has explained, “[s]craping involves extracting data from a website
and copying it into a structured format, allowing for data manipulation or analysis,”
usually by automated means, i.e., a computer script that requests and retrieves
information. hiQ Labs, 31 F.4th at 1186 n.4. Unlike a browser, which requests and retrieves
information for display to an internet user, a scraper requests and retrieves information for
another purpose, often a more tailored one, e.g., to extract and copy the court dates of
inmates published daily by a county jail to help journalists better understand the inmates’
trajectories through the system.

It bears emphasis that this action deals only with scraping data that X Corp. has made
publicly available. X Corp. does not allege or in any way suggest that the data scraped was
solely accessible to X users logged in to registered accounts or was otherwise password-
protected. Rather, it points to materials advertising “techniques to scrape, structure, and
analyze public web data” and “[t]ap into ... public accounts,” as well as tools used to “gather
vast amounts of public web data.” X Corp. “employs rate limits that cap the number of posts
that may be viewed by registered users and those who access the platform without an
account,” but that does not render public posts any less public. Nor do the other “industry
standard automation prevention techniques” that X Corp. implements, such as CAPTCHAs*
and anomaly detection tools.

In addition to the ban on scraping, the Terms provide for other technical restrictions. For
example, an X user may not “access, tamper with, or use non-public areas of the Services,
our computer systems, or the technical delivery systems of our providers.” An X user also
may not “access or search or attempt to access or search the Services by any means
(automated or otherwise) other than through our currently available, published interfaces
that are provided by us (and only pursuant to the applicable terms and conditions), unless
you have been specifically allowed to do so in a separate agreement with us.”



* [Editor’s note: CAPTCHA is an acronym for “Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and

Humans Apart.” It’s the gibberish letters and numbers you are asked to decipher before you can proceed to your
destination, on the theory that humans can decode the gibberish and the bots cannot. As a practical matter, the
bots are pretty good at beating CAPTCHAs, and the price of getting foreign labor (such as from India) to
manually decode CAPTCHAs in bulk is surprisingly low. See Dan Woods, I Was a Human CAPTCHA Solver, F5
(May 13, 2021), https://www.f5.com/labs/articles/cisotociso/i-was-a-human-captcha-solver.]



                                                     109.
Moreover, the Terms restrict an X user from selling data from X. Again, “Content” is
broadly defined as “any information, text, links, graphics, photos, audio, videos, or other
materials or arrangements of materials uploaded, downloaded or appearing on the
Services.” And, an X user may not “sell ... the Services or Content on the Services” unless
otherwise authorized. But, “[f]or developers who wish to retrieve or analyze X Corp.’s data,
X Corp. offers specialized access to its Application Programming Interfaces (‘APIs’) through
a tiered subscription service,” i.e., for a fee. So, X Corp. allows for the sale of data extracted
and copied from X but only if X Corp. is paid for it. X Corp. otherwise restricts the sale of
data extracted and copied from X by prohibiting an X user from scraping and selling data
from the platform.

2. Present Allegations.
Defendant Bright Data Ltd. is a data-scraping company. According to Bright Data, “[i]ts
suite of technologies and services help Fortune 500 companies, academic institutions, and
small businesses retrieve and synthesize vast amounts of public information.” There are
three types of products that Bright Data offers: (1) datasets built from data that Bright
Data scrapes itself, (2) scraping tools that enable their purchasers to scrape data
themselves, and (3) proxy network services that enable their purchasers to scrape data
through proxy servers, using those servers’ IP addresses.

In this lawsuit, X Corp. alleges that Bright Data scrapes data from X and sells data scraped
from X, using elaborate technical measures to evade X Corp.’s anti-scraping technology,
while facilitating its customers in and inducing them to scrape data from X — all in
violation of the Terms to which Bright Data and its customers are bound. How so? X Corp.
contends that Bright Data and its customers are bound as X users. Specifically, X Corp.
contends that Bright Data is bound (1) by a “browser-wrap” or “browse-wrap” contract,*
having used X Corp. services in the act of scraping data from X, impliedly agreeing to the
Terms in the process; and (2) by a “click-wrap” or “click-through” contract, having
registered an account (@bright_data) to promote Bright Data products, expressly agreeing
to the Terms as early as February 2016. Meanwhile, Bright Data customers are conceivably
likewise bound by browser-wrap and click-wrap contracts, having used X Corp. services in
the act of scraping data from X and, in some instances, having registered accounts.

X Corp. does not allege that Bright Data has used its own account, or any other account, to
scrape data from X. Nor does X Corp. allege that Bright Data customers have used their
own accounts, or any other accounts, to do so. All X Corp. alleges is that Bright Data and its
customers have scraped data from X, violating the Terms to which they were bound due to
their use of the services in scraping (forming browser-wrap contracts) and, in some cases,
account registration prior to scraping (forming click-wrap contracts).….

1. Claims Based on Access to Systems.
X Corp.’s interest in the systems accessed is clear cut. Surely, “the analogy between real
property and the internet is not perfect.” But it is now well-established that some exchange
of information across privately owned servers, routers, and networks connected to the
internet can interfere with a personal property interest without depriving the owner of
personal property in the traditional sense. See Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374,
378 (2021).

* [Editor’s note: The court isn’t sure if it’s “browsewrap” or “browser-wrap.” Maybe never use either term?]




                                                       110.
Exchange of information across another’s internet-connected systems is to be expected. The
internet was designed to enable this exchange. Moreover, “a defining feature of public
websites is that their publicly available sections lack limitations on access” and “are open to
anyone with a web browser.” hiQ Labs, 31 F.4th at 1199. Whether some exchange of
information across a social media company’s internet-connected systems can support a
claim for relief is thus contextual. Here, X Corp.’s claims based on access to its internet-
connected systems are not plausibly pleaded.

A. Trespass to Chattels.
We start with trespass to chattels, an old tort that is finding new life. According to X Corp.,
Bright Data “intentionally entered into, and made use of, X Corp.’s technological
infrastructure ... to obtain information for its own economic benefit.” Bright Data thereby
“knowingly exceeded the permission granted by X Corp. to access its personal property” and
“caused other persons ... to knowingly exceed the permission granted by X Corp. to access
its personal property.” X Corp. contends that this “conduct constitutes trespass to X Corp.’s
chattels.”

The Supreme Court of California has held that “trespass to chattels lies where an
intentional interference with the possession of personal property has proximately caused
injury.” Intel Corp. v. Hamidi, 30 Cal.4th 1342 (2003). As such, “an interference (not
amounting to dispossession) is not actionable, under modern California and broader
American law, without a showing of harm.” “Short of dispossession, personal injury, or
physical damage (not present here), intermeddling is actionable only if the chattel is
impaired as to its condition, quality, or value, or ... the possessor is deprived of the use of
the chattel for a substantial time.”

Critically, the instant complaint alleges no such impairment or deprivation. X Corp. parrots
elements, reciting that Bright Data’s “acts have caused injury to X Corp. and ... will cause
damage in the form of impaired condition, quality, and value of its servers, technology
infrastructure, services, and reputation.” Its lone deviation from that parroting — a
conclusory statement that Bright Data’s “acts have diminished the server capacity that X
Corp. can devote to its legitimate users” — fails to move the needle. To say nothing of the
fact that, as alleged, Bright Data and its customers are legitimate X users (subject to the
Terms), the scraping tools and services they use are reliant on X Corp.’s servers functioning
exactly as intended.

Absent allegation, it cannot be assumed that Bright Data or its customers sending requests
to X Corp.’s servers with a scraper is inherently burdensome, or inherently more
burdensome than an X user sending requests to X Corp.’s servers with a browser. After all,
“the load placed on the host’s server may in fact be lighter, because the scraper may only
need one web resource, rather than the dozens a web-browser might need, in order to
extract the relevant information.”

Meanwhile, Intel rejected an attempt to bend trespass to chattels into a claim that could
remedy injury to reputation, warning of “br[eaking] the chain between the trespass and the
harm, allowing indirect harms to [a plaintiff’s] business interests ... to count as harms to
the chattel (the server),” and “cut[ting] trespass to chattels free from its moorings of
dispossession or the equivalent, allowing the court free reign [sic] to hunt for ‘impairment.’”


                                               111.
Intel also held that time and money spent attempting to restrict access cannot be
“bootstrapped into an injury to [a plaintiff’s] possessory interest in its computers,” because
“[i]njury can only be established by the completed tort’s consequences, not by the cost of the
steps taken to avoid the injury and prevent the tort; otherwise, we can create injury for
every supposed tort.” X Corp. should keep all of this in mind if it seeks leave to amend the
instant complaint. In any event, the facts now alleged are insufficient to state a claim for
trespass to chattels.

This order does not hold that sending requests to servers could never support a trespass-to-
chattels claim. By way of example, as our own Judge Edward Chen has observed, denial-of-
service attacks could prove remediable under this tort (inundating servers with requests,
often forcing them offline). See hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 273 F. Supp. 3d 1099, 1113
n.11 (N.D. Cal. 2017). All that has been alleged here, however, is that Bright Data has sent
requests to X Corp. servers in violation of the Terms, which does not itself impair the
servers or deprive X Corp. of their use.

Nor does this order in any way suggest that X Corp. should refrain from implementing
technical measures to restrict access to its systems, e.g., “CAPTCHAs, user identification
and IP rate limits and anomaly detection tools.” Not only does the law decline to forbid such
measures, but it generally allows X Corp. to implement them. As observed in Intel,
“[s]ufficient legal protection of the possessor’s interest in the mere inviolability of his
chattel is afforded by his privilege to use reasonable force to protect his possession against
even harmless interference.” But harmless interference cannot constitute trespass to
chattels…

                                 NOTES AND QUESTIONS

Don’t Property Owners Always Have an Absolute Right to Exclude? Why isn’t it sufficient for
X to say that it objects to Bright Data’s usage of its servers, so Bright Data’s continued
activity is a per se harm? This argument would work for real property trespass, but the
harm requirements for trespass to chattels are more rigorous. In other words, chattel
owners don’t have an absolute right to exclude others without a showing of sufficient harm.

The availability of Twitter’s paid API access proves to be irrelevant to this inquiry. If Bright
Data cannot be legally excluded from accessing Twitter, then Twitter cannot force Bright
Data into the API access. There are no lost revenues from unpaid API access fees because
Twitter wasn’t legally entitled to those fees.

What About X’s TOS? X included multiple redundant provisions in its TOS to restrict
Bright Data’s activity. Why didn’t that work?

Bright Data created a Twitter account in 2016, but by the time of the lawsuit, it claims it
had terminated its account—and thus was no longer bound by the TOS. X counterargued
that Bright Data agreed to X’s “browsewrap” by accessing its service. (As you saw, the
browsewrap/”browserwrap” terminology flummoxed the court). Normally, browsewraps fail
easily, but the court says Bright Data is “a party with actual knowledge of the Terms at all
relevant times (and a sophisticated party to boot),” and that knowledge supports contract
formation. Nevertheless, X’s contract claim failed for lack of damages: “X Corp. has not
alleged any damage resulting from access through unauthorized means, merely alluding to


                                              112.
diminished capacity and reputational harm without pleading any impairment or
deprivation of servers.”

What About Other Trespass to Chattels Claims? The court only analyzed the common law
trespass to chattels claim. If X brought CFAA or California Penal Code 502 claims, would
those claims reach different results?

Technological Self-Help. The court says: “this order does not in any way suggest that X
Corp. should refrain from engaging in ‘technological self-help’ to restrict access to its
systems.” In other words, X can take whatever technological steps it chooses to block Bright
Data’s activity. That may seem obvious—of course X has the freedom to engage in self-help.
However, the hiQ court temporarily blocked LinkedIn’s technological self-help, giving hiQ
essentially unrestricted access to LinkedIn’s servers and the data available on it (LinkedIn
eventually won that case and could reinstate its self-help efforts). What technological
blocking efforts can X take, and what legal recourse should X have if Bright Data figures
out how to bypass those blocks?

Note the relevance of technological self-help in any request for equitable relief. If a trespass
to chattels plaintiff hasn’t taken easy self-help steps, a court is less likely to feel like it
needs to award equitable relief. In contrast, some courts (especially outside of California)
will be more inclined to provide equitable remedies if a chattel owner has taken all
reasonable self-help efforts and those steps didn’t solve its problem.

What About Bright Data’s Sales of Data Collected from X? The court says that all claims
based on Bright Data’s sale of scraped data failed due to copyright preemption. X lacks
standing to enforce the copyrights in its users’ content. Thus, “invoking state contract and
tort law, X Corp. would entrench its own private copyright system that rivals, even conflicts
with, the actual copyright system enacted by Congress. X Corp. would yank into its private
domain and hold for sale information open to all, exercising a copyright owner’s right to
exclude where it has no such right…We are instead concerned with a massive regime of
adhesive terms imposed by X Corp. that stands to fundamentally alter the rights and
privileges of the world at large (or at least hundreds of millions of alleged X users).”

IP Address Proxies. Bright Data has a separate service to help its customers mask their IP
addresses, which enables those customers’ scraping activities to bypass X’s attempts to IP
address-block them. The court isn’t bothered by this cat-and-mouse game:

       X Corp. appears to insinuate that the use of different IP addresses is
       inherently deceptive. But an internet user is not assigned a unique IP
       address. Rather, as our court of appeals has explained, “[e]very computer or
       server connected to the Internet has a unique IP address.” Accordingly,
       internet users can have different IP addresses simply by virtue of using
       different devices (e.g., smartphone, laptop, desktop) across different
       connections (e.g., cellular network, home network, work network). Internet
       users can also change the IP addresses they use to request and retrieve
       information (e.g., using virtual private networks). What’s more, “IP addresses
       can be dynamic,” with “the number chang[ing] each time the computer
       accesses the Internet.” None of this is inherently deceptive….



                                              113.
       There is no affirmative duty that requires an internet user to identify oneself
       with a given IP address when connecting to the internet, however. “[A]
       failure to disclose a fact one has no affirmative duty to disclose is [not] ‘likely
       to deceive’ anyone.”

Does This Ruling Mean Scrapers Get a Free Pass? The court gave X the ability to replead its
complaint. Perhaps it will make better allegations in its second go-around. This opinion
certainly doesn’t categorically permit scraping. Indeed, the opinion expressly says it “does
not hold that sending requests to servers could never support a trespass-to-chattels claim.”
Nevertheless, the court made several moves that makes anti-scraping lawsuits harder to
win, including looking at the impact of scraping queries compared to the impact of ordinary
browsing and saying copyright preempts claims based on sales of the scraped data.

The Intel v. Hamidi Decision. Intel Corp. v. Hamidi, 30 Cal. 4th 1342 (Cal. 2003) (referred
to as the “Intel” case in the Bright Data opinion), is an OG Internet Law classic opinion and
was a casebook stalwart for twenty years. Anyone pursuing an Internet Law career must
read the opinion; it contains a rich set of policy discussions and a wonderful snapshot of
Internet Law circa the turn of the century.

The Hamidi case involved a disgruntled Intel ex-employee, Hamidi, who encouraged then-
current Intel employees to resist Intel’s allegedly abusive practices. (At the time, critics like
Hamidi were called “gripers”). Hamidi came into possession of a list of current employees’
email addresses, which he used six times to send unsolicited emails criticizing Intel through
Intel’s email routers. Though Intel’s routers could easily handle Hamidi’s incoming bulk
emails, Intel claimed that the emails distracted its employees. In a sense, Intel’s argument
treated its employees’ time as the employer’s chattel, a problematic framing from a policy
perspective.

Intel sought an injunction against further Hamidi emails based solely on the common law
trespass to chattels. A divided California Supreme Court rejected the request, saying that
Hamidi didn’t cause legally recognizable harm. Instead, the majority said that common law
trespass to chattels is actionable only when electronic signals cause or threaten to cause
measurable loss to computer system resources. Thus, Hamidi’s disturbance of Intel’s
employees had no relevance to the claim. Instead, Intel “demonstrated neither any
appreciable effect on the operation of its computer system from Hamidi’s message, nor any
likelihood that Hamidi’s actions will be replicated by others if found not to constitute a
trespass.”

The Hamidi precedent remains the prevailing law in California, and it influences the
Bright Data court. However, overall, the Hamidi decision has waned in import for two
reasons. First, other jurisdictions have taken a more plaintiff-favorable view of the
common law doctrine, often finding recognizable harm to the chattel based on negligible
impacts or deeming there to be a higher risk of copycat misusers than in Hamidi. Second,
and more importantly, the CFAA has eclipsed the common law doctrine in importance, so
most plaintiffs bring a CFAA claim (which Intel did not do) and focus on its slightly
different standards.




                                               114.
The Van Buren Decision. In 2021, the U.S. Supreme Court substantively reviewed the
CFAA for the first time. Van Buren v. U.S., 141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021). Overall, the majority
opinion read the CFAA narrowly, but it left open many key questions.

Van Buren was a law enforcement officer who accepted a bribe to deliver private
information from a computer database restricted to law enforcement. As part of his job, he
generally had right to use his computing device to connect to the restricted database and
make the search query. However, his actions were outside the scope of his job duties
(indeed, they likely violated department policies). The question is whether his conduct
criminally violated the CFAA.

To prove the crime, the government had to show that Van Buren’s use of his computing
device and search of the database “exceeded authorized access.” The court said he did not:

       an individual “exceeds authorized access” when he accesses a computer with
       authorization but then obtains information located in particular areas of the
       computer—such as files, folders, or databases—that are off limits to him. The
       parties agree that Van Buren accessed the law enforcement database system
       with authorization. The only question is whether Van Buren could use the
       system to retrieve license-plate information. Both sides agree that he could.
       Van Buren accordingly did not “excee[d] authorized access” to the database,
       as the CFAA defines that phrase, even though he obtained information from
       the database for an improper purpose

The parties’ concessions allowed the court to reach a narrow and fact-specific conclusion.
But the court’s statements raise obvious questions: (1) what makes a particular computer
area “off-limits,” and (2) what facts confirm that a user knew about those limits? The court
did not clearly answer either question.

In determining what areas are “off-limits,” the opinion suggests it matters if “gates” are “up
or down,” but gave no extra clarity on what constitutes a “gate” or how we’ll know if it’s up
or down. The court also didn’t specify if “gates down” (the portcullis analogy) or “gates up”
(the fence analogy) means a chattel owner successfully delimited access.

The court expresses concern about contracts as delimiters of authorization:

       If the “exceeds authorized access” clause criminalizes every violation of a
       computer-use policy, then millions of otherwise law-abiding citizens are
       criminals. Take the workplace. Employers commonly state that computers
       and electronic devices can be used only for business purposes. So on the
       Government’s reading of the statute, an employee who sends a personal e-
       mail or reads the news using her work computer has violated the CFAA. Or
       consider the Internet. Many websites, services, and databases—which
       provide “information” from “protected computer[s]”—authorize a user’s access
       only upon his agreement to follow specified terms of service. If the “exceeds
       authorized access” clause encompasses violations of circumstance-based
       access restrictions on employers’ computers, it is difficult to see why it would
       not also encompass violations of such restrictions on website providers’
       computers.


                                             115.
Yet, FN8 of the opinion says “we need not address whether this inquiry turns only on
technological (or ‘code-based’) limitations on access, or instead also looks to limits contained
in contracts or policies.” So if a user violates a website TOS, did the user exceed authorized
access? The opinion expressly didn’t answer that question.

The limited helpfulness of the court’s opinion become even more apparent by reviewing
some other examples of what might constitute a “gate”:

      Cease & Desist (C&D) letters. Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058
       (9th Cir. 2016), held that “a defendant can run afoul of the CFAA when he or she has
       no permission to access a computer or when such permission has been revoked
       explicitly,” and a C&D letter was sufficient to revoke permission. Did this case
       survive Van Buren? It would be weird if a binding TOS with mutual assent might
       not restrict access, but a unilaterally drafted C&D—which the recipient has never
       agreed to—could. Cf. Meta Platforms, Inc. v. BrandTotal, Ltd., 605 F. Supp. 3d 1218
       (N.D. Cal. 2022) (Facebook’s complaint withdrew consent).
      Password Protection. When a service puts content or functionality behind a
       password “wall,” does that mean the gates are in place? It seems like password
       protection should be the paradigmatic example of a “technological limitations on
       access,” so accessing the password-protected areas without any permission should
       trigger the CFAA. However, what happens if the user legitimately obtains a
       password but then engages in rogue activity? That’s essentially the Van Buren facts.
       With respect to non-employees, any permissions associated with the password would
       be stated in the applicable TOS, but the court questioned if TOS restrictions can
       delimit permission. Now what?
      IP Address Blocks. IP address blocks also seem like technological limitations on
       access, but what exactly is restricted? For example, does the block apply only the
       specific IP address blocked? If so, in theory the user can just obtain a new IP address
       and proceed without any restriction. That’s apparently what Bright Data did,
       seemingly with the court’s blessing. Or does the IP address block tell the user that
       any further access is unauthorized, even from different IP addresses? How does a
       user know their IP address was blocked? That may merge into the discussion of
       whether C&Ds can delimit access.
      Robot Exclusion Headers (REH, also called robots.txt). REHs are machine-readable
       instructions to robots about what the server owner permits them to do on the site.
       Robots aren’t required to consult the headers and can ignore any provided
       instructions, but polite robots respect those instructions. Do REH constitute “gates”?

An example of a robots.txt file (from https://www.sitejabber.com/robots.txt):




                                              116.
(Invariably, there is a story behind each instruction added to a robots.txt file).

Employers routinely use the CFAA to sue departing employees for taking electronic files
with them as they leave, either on a flash drive or by sending the files to themselves
electronically (such as via email or uploading the files to their personal cloud storage).
(These file grabs may also violate trade secret and other laws). If the employees had
legitimate access to those files as part of their jobs, will the CFAA still apply to those
circumstances? After all, there are no technological gates restricting their access. Would it
matter if the employer had a provision in its standard employment agreement restricting
such activity? Or if the employer, anticipating the departure, warned the employee not to
take any electronic files?

Subsequent Ruling in X v. Bright Data. X amended the complaint and revived its trespass
to chattels claim. The court said that X sufficiently stated harm from Bright Data’s
scraping when it alleged that:

(1) “scrapers traverse the X service in patterns markedly different from humans or
authorized machines, that scrapers thus use underlying server capacity in abnormal
proportions, and that this results in intermittent, isolated server failures and a “glitchy,
lagged user experience” for X’s human users.” Specifically, X alleged that “each scraper is
‘at least’ a million times more burdensome than an ordinary user.”

(2) “but for X Corp.’s purchase of millions of dollars of server capacity, this conduct would
result in catastrophic system failures.” The court says that this alleges sufficient financial
harm, i.e., that “X Corp. spends money to replace or supplement its property that is or soon




                                              117.
would be functionally impaired: It pays for 10–20% more server capacity than that which,
but for the tortious conduct, would be needed.”

(3) “Bright Data bears the blame for this profusion of scraping as an industry leader, even if
the exact amount it contributes is now knowable only to it.”

The court also said that X sufficiently alleged that it had withdrawn any authorization that
Bright Data may have had. The court summarizes: “Bright Data allegedly exceeded the
limits X imposes on all users alike through Terms and technical measures — despite
receiving notice in both manners that any authorization it had enjoyed was now rejected.”

X Corp. v. Bright Data Ltd., 2024 WL 4894290 (N.D. Cal. 2024).

                           CHAPTER 4 REVIEW QUESTION #1

Karen creates an online bank account for herself and agrees to the bank’s Terms of Service,
which include a provision saying that customers may not provide their online login
credentials to the bank account to anyone. Despite this, Karen shares her credentials with
her live-in boyfriend, Joe. Scenario (a): Joe logs into the bank account to engage in ordinary
banking activities at Karen’s request. Scenario (b): Joe logs into the bank account and loots
it, sending all of the money to his personal bank account. Does the bank have a CFAA claim
against either Joe or Karen?




                                             118.
                                     V.      Copyright

Copyright Basics, Copyright Office Circular 1 (from
https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ01.pdf) (revised Sept. 2017)

Copyright is a form of protection provided by the laws of the United States to the authors of
“original works of authorship” that are fixed in a tangible form of expression. An original
work of authorship is a work that is independently created by a human author and
possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity. A work is “fixed” when it is captured
(either by or under the authority of an author) in a sufficiently permanent medium such
that the work can be perceived, reproduced, or communicated for more than a short time.
Copyright protection in the United States exists automatically from the moment the
original work of authorship is fixed.

What Works Are Protected?

Examples of copyrightable works include
• Literary works
• Musical works, including any accompanying words
• Dramatic works, including any accompanying music
• Pantomimes and choreographic works
• Pictorial, graphic, and sculptural works
• Motion pictures and other audiovisual works
• Sound recordings, which are works that result from the fixation of a series of musical,
spoken, or other sounds
• Architectural works

These categories should be viewed broadly for the purpose of registering your work. For
example, computer programs and certain “compilations” can be registered as “literary
works”; maps and technical drawings can be registered as “pictorial, graphic, and
sculptural works.”

Note: Before 1978, federal copyright was generally secured by publishing a work with an
appropriate copyright notice. U.S. works that were in the public domain on January 1,
1978, when the 1976 Copyright Act took effect, remain in the public domain under the 1976
Act.

What Are the Rights of a Copyright Owner?

Copyright provides the owner of copyright with the exclusive right to
• Reproduce the work in copies or phonorecords
• Prepare derivative works based upon the work
• Distribute copies or phonorecords of the work to the public by sale or other transfer of
ownership or by rental, lease, or lending
• Perform the work publicly if it is a literary, musical, dramatic, or choreographic work; a
pantomime; or a motion picture or other audiovisual work
• Display the work publicly if it is a literary, musical, dramatic, or choreographic work; a
pantomime; or a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work. This right also applies to the
individual images of a motion picture or other audiovisual work.


                                             119.
• Perform the work publicly by means of a digital audio transmission if the work is a sound
recording

Copyright also provides the owner of copyright the right to authorize others to exercise
these exclusive rights, subject to certain statutory limitations.

What Is Not Protected by Copyright?

Copyright does not protect
• Ideas, procedures, methods, systems, processes, concepts, principles, or discoveries
• Works that are not fixed in a tangible form (such as a choreographic work that has not
been notated or recorded or an improvisational speech that has not been written down)
• Titles, names, short phrases, and slogans
• Familiar symbols or designs
• Mere variations of typographic ornamentation, lettering, or coloring
• Mere listings of ingredients or contents…

Who Can Claim Copyright?

The copyright in a work initially belongs to the author(s) who created that work. When two
or more authors create a single work with the intent of merging their contributions into
inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole, the authors are considered joint
authors and have an indivisible interest in the work as a whole. By contrast, if multiple
authors contribute to a collective work, each author’s individual contribution is separate
and distinct from the copyright ownership in the collective work as a whole.

“Works made for hire” are an important exception to the general rule for claiming
copyright. When a work is made for hire, the author is not the individual who actually
created the work. Instead, the party that hired the individual is considered the author and
the copyright owner of the work. Whether a work is made for hire is determined by the facts
that exist at the time the work is created. There are two situations in which a work may be
made for hire:

1. When the work is created by an employee as part of the employee’s regular duties, or
2. When an individual and the hiring party enter into an express written agreement that
the work is to be considered a “work made for hire” and the work is specially ordered or
commissioned for use as:
• A compilation
• A contribution to a collective work
• A part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work
• A translation
• A supplementary work
• An instructional text
• A test
• Answer material for a test
• An atlas




                                             120.
The concept of work made for hire can be complicated and has serious consequences for
both the individual who creates the work and the hiring party who is considered to be the
author and copyright owner of the work.…

Note: Mere ownership of a copy or phonorecord that embodies a work does not give the
owner of that copy or phonorecord the ownership of the copyright in the work.

Transfer of Copyright Ownership

Any or all of the copyright owner’s exclusive rights, or parts of those rights, can be
transferred. The transfer, however, generally must be made in writing and signed by the
owner of the rights conveyed or the owner’s authorized agent. Transferring a right on a
nonexclusive basis does not require a written agreement….

How Long Does Copyright Last?

In general, for works created on or after January 1, 1978, the term of copyright is the life of
the author plus seventy years after the author’s death. If the work is a joint work with
multiple authors, the term lasts for seventy years after the last surviving author’s death.
For works made for hire and anonymous or pseudonymous works, the duration of copyright
is 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation, whichever is shorter….

How Can I Protect My Work?

Copyright exists automatically in an original work of authorship once it is fixed in a
tangible medium, but a copyright owner can take steps to enhance the protections of
copyright, the most important of which is registering the work. Although registering a work
is not mandatory, for works of U.S. origin, registration (or refusal) is necessary to enforce
the exclusive rights of copyright through litigation….

Using a copyright notice is optional for unpublished works, foreign works, and works
published on or after March 1, 1989….Notice was required for works published in the
United States before March 1, 1989. Works published without notice before that date may
have entered the public domain in this country….

How Can I Use a Copyrighted Work?

When deciding to use a work protected by copyright, the general rule is to seek permission
from the copyright owner. Under the copyright law, a copyright owner may authorize
activities that fall under the exclusive rights of copyright…

Sections 107 to 122 of the copyright law contain provisions that establish limitations on the
exclusive rights of the copyright owner. The provisions make certain uses of copyrighted
works permissible without first obtaining permission of the copyright owner. One of the
most discussed of these statutory provisions is known as fair use, a legal doctrine that
promotes freedom of expression by permitting the unlicensed use of copyright-protected
works in certain circumstances….




                                              121.
How Do I Protect My Work in Other Countries?

There is no such thing as an “international copyright” that automatically protects an
author’s works throughout the entire world. Protection against unauthorized use in a
particular country depends on the national laws of that country. Most countries offer
protection to foreign works under certain conditions, and these conditions have been greatly
simplified by international copyright treaties and conventions. Generally, a U.S. work may
be protected in a foreign country if that country has entered into an international
agreement with the United States….

                                NOTES AND QUESTIONS

“Access” to Online Materials. Unless the defendant admits to copying the plaintiff’s work, a
copyright plaintiff normally needs to show that the defendant had “access” to the
copyrighted work as part of disproving that the defendant independently created the work
(unlike patent law, copyright law permits independent creation). The logic goes: if the
defendant had access to the work, then we can sometimes infer that the defendant copied
the plaintiff’s work rather than independently creating it.

In the Internet era, a work posted online is nominally accessible to everyone in the world.
(Some works have restricted access behind paywalls or registration walls, something that
the courts haven’t fully wrestled with yet). As a result, courts could say that every
defendant always has “access” to any copyrighted work posted to the Internet, in which case
plaintiffs who’ve publicly posted their works automatically satisfy this element of their
prima facie copyright infringement case.

Courts do not go that far. As the Seventh Circuit has said, “the existence of the plaintiff’s
copyrighted materials on the Internet, even on a public and ‘user‐friendly’ site, cannot by
itself justify an inference that the defendant accessed those materials.” Design Basics, LLC
v. Lexington Homes, Inc., 858 F.3d 1093 (7th Cir. 2017).

In a case involving allegedly imitative photos on Instagram (Woodland is the plaintiff, Hill
is the defendant), the Ninth Circuit explained:

       While standalone websites make content available to anyone in the world,
       digital platforms do that and more. Digital platforms create online
       communities and actively connect content creators with content consumers.
       Platforms like Instagram are designed to facilitate the discovery and sharing
       of available content by using algorithms to recommend tailored content to
       consumers. No longer do people have to search for specific content in the vast
       expanse of the Internet; in today’s digital landscape, social media networks
       and other platforms continually push individualized content to consumers
       based on each individual’s preferences, usage, and habits. And by expanding
       a content creator’s reach, these digital platforms can increase the chances
       that other people will see—i.e., have access to—the creator’s copyrighted
       content.




                                             122.
        Consider the proverbial pajama-clad blogger from the early 2000s* who would
        share his musings on his personal Internet blog while sitting in his mother’s
        basement. Unless someone intentionally searched for that blog website,
        almost no one (except perhaps his hapless mother who encouraged him to go
        outside and find gainful employment) would have likely viewed his blog
        posts, even though theoretically they were available to everyone. But in the
        age of Twitter/X and other content-sharing platforms, that erstwhile blogger’s
        reach could multiply dramatically as others’ “views” and “likes” on Twitter/X
        may push his posts to a larger audience under that platform’s algorithm.
        Indeed, content from an ordinary person with a few followers can now go
        “viral” and reach millions of people.

        It is no wonder why, then, in the “digitally interconnected world” of online
        platforms “the concept of ‘access’ is increasingly diluted.” To sum up, social
        media and other digital-sharing platforms could make it easier for plaintiffs
        to show that defendants had access to their materials—but only if they can
        show that the defendants had a reasonable chance of seeing their work under
        that platform’s algorithm or content- sharing policy. That is a big “if”—and,
        as explained below, Woodland has fallen short here.

        While Instagram may make a user’s content more widely accessible, it is not
        enough to simply allege that Hill is an active user of Instagram and thus had
        a reasonable possibility of viewing Woodland’s photos. As the district court
        explained, there are over a billion users and many more posts on Instagram.
        The mere fact that Hill uses Instagram and that Woodland’s photos are on
        Instagram raises no more than a “bare possibility” that Hill viewed
        Woodland’s photos…

        Woodland’s sources explain that Instagram suggests posts based on the
        accounts that users follow; the posts users like, share, and comment on;
        users’ history of connecting with accounts; and how popular a particular post
        is and how others have interacted with that post. We need not decide today
        what precise facts a plaintiff must allege about a digital platform’s algorithm
        or content-sharing policy to show “access.” But we can say that Woodland has
        not sufficiently pleaded that Hill had access to his Instagram photos, given
        that he does not plausibly allege that Hill followed, liked, or otherwise
        interacted with posts or accounts connected to or similar to Woodland.

Woodland v. Hill, 136 F.4th 1199 (9th Cir. 2025).

While the Woodland ruling benefited the defense, the court invites plaintiffs to present
evidence that the defense had “followed, liked, or otherwise interacted with posts or
accounts connected to or similar to” the plaintiff’s. Plaintiffs can mine defendants’ social
media engagement to find such evidence—even if it’s tendentious or circumstantial—which
creates the risk that this standard will help unmeritorious cases survive a little longer or
otherwise raise defense costs.

* [Editor’s note: I felt personally targeted by this analogy, though I was living in my own home by the time I

started blogging.]



                                                       123.
Statute of Limitations. Copyright has a 3 year statute of limitations. However, the time
period does not start on initial publication to the web; instead, it resets with every
infringing act, such as every view or download. Thus, works posted to the Internet decades
ago may be the basis of copyright infringement claims if the works are still online. See APL
Microscopic, LLC v. U.S., 144 Fed. Cl. 489 (Ct. Fed. Claims 2019).

The Copyright Claims Board. In 2022, the Copyright Office launched a “small claims court”
for copyright disputes called the “Copyright Claims Board,” or CCB. The CCB gives
copyright owners an alternative venue to federal courts to enforce their works. The CCB
limits a copyright owner’s potential damages (maximum possibility of $15,000 per work and
$30,000 in a single proceeding), and copyright owners may bring no more than 30 CCB
proceedings per year. To expedite the cases, discovery and appeals are limited. A defendant
can opt-out of the proceeding within 60 days of getting notice, in which case the copyright
owner must either refile in federal court or drop the matter.
