technology did not include any effective method ... to prevent minors from obtaining access
... without also denying access to adults.” The CDA thus triggered—and failed—strict
scrutiny because it “effectively suppresse[d] a large amount of speech that adults have a
constitutional right to receive” and to share. This kind of ban is categorically different from
H. B. 1181’s age-verification requirement.

Ashcroft II likewise characterized COPA as a ban. COPA criminally prohibited posting
“content that is ‘harmful to minors’ “ online for “ ‘commercial purposes,’ “ subject to an age-
verification affirmative defense. We thus applied strict scrutiny, because, as in Reno, the
statute “ ‘effectively suppresse[d] a large amount of speech that adults have a constitutional
right to receive and to address to one another.’ “ Because the parties agreed that strict
scrutiny applied, the Court’s discussion of the applicable standard was brief. But, its
wording was careful. The Government in Ashcroft II conceded that COPA triggered strict
scrutiny because it “regulates expression ... that is constitutionally protected for adults ...



                                              282.
on the basis of its content.” Petitioners make essentially that same argument here. Yet, the
Court did not endorse this sweeping proposition; instead, it invoked the narrower ground
that COPA outright “ ‘suppresse[d]’” speech between adults.

To be sure, COPA established an age-verification defense. But, because it did so only as an
affirmative defense, COPA still operated as a ban on the public posting of material that is
obscene to minors. This was so because an indictment need only “alleg[e] the necessary
elements of an offense”; it need not “anticipate affirmative defenses.” Under COPA, the
Government thus remained free to bring criminal charges against any covered person who
publicly posted speech that was obscene to minors, even if he had fully implemented
compliant age-verification procedures. The same is not true under H. B. 1181, which makes
the lack of age verification an element that the State must plead and prove.

2
Petitioners read Reno and Ashcroft II to establish a comprehensive framework to govern all
future attempts to restrict children’s access to online pornography. As we have just
explained, that view cannot be squared with those cases, which addressed only outright
bans on material that was obscene to minors but not to adults. Petitioners also fail to
appreciate the context in which those cases were decided. This Court decided both cases
when the internet was “still more of a prototype than a finished product”—Reno in 1997
and Ashcroft II in 2004, with factual findings made in 1999. We were mindful that “judicial
answers” to “the totally new problems” presented by new technology are necessarily
“truncated,” and that in such circumstances “we ought not to anticipate” questions beyond
those immediately presented. We did not purport to decide more than the specific
circumstances of the cases that were before us.

The Court in Reno was quite concerned about the unique threat that the CDA posed to the
development of the then-nascent internet. Reno was this Court’s first decision about the
internet. In describing the background of the case, we “felt the need to explain ... that the
‘Internet is an international network of interconnected computers,’ “ and we marveled that
the internet had grown to 40 million users worldwide. In resolving the case, the Court was
keenly aware that the “wholly unprecedented” “breadth of the CDA’s coverage”
“threaten[ed] to torch a large segment” of this emerging medium of communication. In
these uncharted waters, the Court was cautious not to definitively establish when
regulations on internet pornography triggered strict scrutiny.

Similarly, Ashcroft II was a self-consciously narrow and factbound decision. There, the
Court reviewed a preliminary injunction based on a record that was “over five years” old, all
while the “technology of the Internet” continued to “evolv[e] at a rapid pace.” As a result, we
emphasized the abuse-of-discretion standard and made clear that we did not mean to rule
definitively on COPA’s constitutionality. Moreover, we could not have meant to offer a
comprehensive discussion on the appropriate standard of scrutiny for laws protecting
children from sexual content online, given that the appropriate standard was not even a
contested issue in the case.

In the quarter century since the factual record closed in Ashcroft II, the internet has
expanded exponentially. In 1999, only two out of five American households had home
internet access. Nearly all those households used a desktop computer or laptop to connect to
the internet, and most used a dial-up connection. Connecting through dial-up came with


                                             283.
significant limitations: Dial-up is much slower than a modern broadband connection, and
because dial-up relied on the home’s phone line, many households could not use the
internet and make or receive phone calls at the same time. And, “video-on-demand” was
largely just a notion that figures like “Bill Gates and Al Gore rhapsodize[d] about”; “most
Netizens would [have] be[en] happy with a system fast enough to view static photos without
waiting an age.”

In contrast, in 2024, 95 percent of American teens had access to a smartphone, allowing
many to access the internet at almost any time and place. Ninety-three percent of teens
reported using the internet several times per day, and watching videos is among their most
common activities online. The content easily accessible to adolescents online includes
massive libraries of pornographic videos. For instance, in 2019, Pornhub, one of the
websites involved in this case, published 1.36 million hours—or over 150 years—of new
content. Many of these readily accessible videos portray men raping and physically
assaulting women—a far cry from the still images that made up the bulk of online
pornography in the 1990s. The Court in Reno and Ashcroft II could not have conceived of
these developments, much less conclusively resolve how States could address them.

Of course, Reno and Ashcroft II do not cease to be precedential simply because technology
has changed so dramatically. “But respect for past judgments also means respecting their
limits.” It is misleading in the extreme to assume that Reno and Ashcroft II spoke to the
circumstances of this case simply because they both dealt with “the internet” as it existed in
the 1990s. The appropriate standard of scrutiny to apply in this case is a difficult question
that no prior decision of this Court has squarely addressed. For the reasons we have
explained, we hold today that H. B. 1181 triggers only intermediate scrutiny.

                                              D

The dissent’s arguments for strict scrutiny are no more persuasive than petitioners’. The
dissent claims that strict scrutiny applies because H. B. 1181 is “a quintessential content-
based law.” We agree that H. B. 1181 targets speech that is obscene for minors based on its
communicative content. But, where the speech in question is unprotected, States may
impose “restrictions” based on “content” without triggering strict scrutiny. Because speech
that is obscene to minors is unprotected to the extent that the State imposes only an age-
verification requirement, H. B. 1181’s content-based restriction does not require strict
scrutiny. The law is content based in the same way that prohibitions of “defamation,”
“fraud,” and “incitement” are.

The dissent’s attempt to distinguish O’Brien and its progeny fails for the same reason. The
dissent protests that H. B. 1181 cannot trigger intermediate scrutiny under O’Brien
because it is “a direct regulation of speech,” not “a regulation of conduct” that incidentally
burdens “expressive activity.” When speech has both protected and unprotected features,
however, “the unprotected features of the [speech] are, despite their [communicative]
character, essentially a ‘nonspeech’ element” for purposes of the First Amendment. With
that principle in hand, H. B. 1181 fits comfortably within the O’Brien framework: The law
directly regulates unprotected activity (accessing material that is obscene to minors without
submitting to age verification) while only incidentally burdening protected activity
(ultimately accessing that material).



                                             284.
The dissent’s real point of disagreement is whether an age-verification requirement
regulates the protected speech of adults. On this point, the dissent has nothing to offer
aside from the bald assertion that our precedents have held as much. But, our precedents
have held no such thing. Because our previous decisions concerned only outright bans, this
Court has never before considered whether lesser burdens aimed at distinguishing children
from adults directly regulate any free speech right of adults.12

Instead, as we have explained, the First Amendment leaves undisturbed States’ power to
impose age limits on speech that is obscene to minors. That power, according to both
“common sense” and centuries of legal tradition, includes the ordinary and appropriate
means of exercising it. And, an age-verification requirement is an ordinary and appropriate
means of enforcing an age limit, as is evident both from all other contexts where the law
draws lines based on age and from the long, widespread, and unchallenged practice of
requiring age verification for in-person sales of material that is obscene to minors. Beyond
misreading precedent, the dissent’s only other response to our reasoning is to assert that
age verification is not necessarily included in the power to draw an age-based line because
“an age verification mandate burdens an adult’s First Amendment” rights. That response
simply assumes what the dissent sets out to prove.

The dissent expresses surprise that obscenity for minors is “only partially” protected speech
for adults. But, it does not truly deny that this is the case. The defendant in Ginsberg, after
all, was an adult vendor of pornography, not an underage purchaser. It would be difficult,
practically speaking, for States to restrict children’s access to pornography without
regulating adult vendors. And, Ginsberg accordingly held that New York’s content-based
restriction on the rights of adult vendors triggered only rational-basis review. Thus, so long
as the dissent accepts Ginsberg, it cannot deny that the question before us is which content-
based regulations States may impose on adults without triggering strict scrutiny, not
whether they may do so.

Finally, the dissent claims that we engage in “backwards,” results-oriented reasoning
because we are unwilling to adopt a position that would call into question the
constitutionality of longstanding in-person age-verification requirements. Not so. We appeal
to these requirements because they embody a constitutional judgment—made by
generations of legislators and by the American people as a whole—that commands our
respect. A decision “contrary to long and unchallenged practice ... should be approached
with great caution,” “no less than an explicit overruling” of a precedent. It would be
perverse if we showed less regard for in-person age-verification requirements simply
because their legitimacy is so uncontroversial that the need for a judicial decision upholding
them has never arisen.

                                                        E

Texas, like the Fifth Circuit, contends that intermediate scrutiny is too demanding and that
only rational-basis review applies. This position fails to account for the incidental burden

12 The dissent is correct that, for fully protected speech, “the distinction between bans and burdens makes no

difference to the level of scrutiny.” But, when the First Amendment partially protects speech, such that the
government may impose certain content-based restrictions on it but may not proscribe it outright, the
distinction between a ban and lesser burdens is meaningful.



                                                       285.
that age verification necessarily has on an adult’s First Amendment right to access speech
that is obscene only to minors. Rational basis is the appropriate standard for laws that do
not implicate “fundamental constitutional rights” at all. Intermediate scrutiny, which is
deferential but not toothless, plays an important role in ensuring that legislatures do not
use ostensibly legitimate purposes to disguise efforts to suppress fundamental rights.

Despite advocating for rational-basis review, Texas itself has acknowledged the need for
more searching review. The State concedes, for instance, that it could not require as proof of
age an “affidavit” from the individual’s “biological parent.” That example is precisely the
sort of manipulation of a legitimate kind of regulation that intermediate scrutiny can weed
out but that rational-basis review cannot.

Texas argues that Ginsberg establishes that age-verification requirements receive only
rational-basis review. But, although Ginsberg applied that standard to a statute with an
age-verification requirement, the Court did not squarely address the incidental effect that
the law had on adults’ First Amendment rights. Moreover, Ginsberg was decided before this
Court first articulated the intermediate-scrutiny standard for incidental burdens on free
speech. In a two-tiered framework, where the only options were strict scrutiny and rational-
basis review, the latter was the better standard for an age-verification requirement.

                                               IV

A statute survives intermediate scrutiny if it “advances important governmental interests
unrelated to the suppression of free speech and does not burden substantially more speech
than necessary to further those interests.” H. B. 1181 readily satisfies these requirements.

                                                A

H. B. 1181 undoubtedly advances an important governmental interest. Texas’s interest in
shielding children from sexual content is important, even “compelling.” H. B. 1181 furthers
that interest by preventing minors from easily circumventing a prohibition on their
accessing sexual content.

H. B. 1181 is also sufficiently tailored to Texas’s interest. Under intermediate scrutiny, a
regulation is adequately tailored so long as the government’s interest “would be achieved
less effectively absent the regulation” and the regulation “does not burden substantially
more speech than is necessary to further that interest.” The regulation “need not be the
least restrictive ... means of “ serving the State’s interest. And, the regulation’s validity “
‘does not turn on [our] agreement with the [legislature] concerning the most appropriate
method for promoting significant government interests’ or the degree to which those
interests should be promoted.”

Under this standard, requiring age verification online is plainly a legitimate legislative
choice. Since at least the days of Ginsberg, States have commonly used age-verification
requirements, in the case of in-person access to sexual materials, to reconcile their interest
in protecting children with adults’ right to avail themselves of such materials. This
approach ensures that an age-based ban is not ineffectual, while at the same time allowing
adults full access to the content in question after the modest burden of providing proof of
age. H. B. 1181 simply adapts this traditional approach to the digital age.


                                               286.
The specific verification methods that H. B. 1181 permits are also plainly legitimate. At
present, H. B. 1181 allows for verification using government-issued identification or
transactional data. Verification can take place on the covered website itself or through a
third-party service. Other age-restricted services, such as online gambling, alcohol and
tobacco sales, and car rentals, rely on the same methods. And, much of the online
pornography industry has used analogous methods for decades. In Reno, this Court
observed that age verification through credit-card transactions “is not only technologically
available but actually is used by commercial providers of sexually explicit material,” who
(unlike many of the noncommercial sites covered by the CDA) “ ‘would remain relatively
unaffected’ “ were such verification required. The District Court in Ashcroft II found that
the users of tens of thousands of pornographic websites verified their ages by submitting “a
copy of a passport or driver’s license” to a third-party verification service. H. B. 1181 simply
requires established verification methods already in use by pornographic sites and other
industries. That choice is well within the State’s discretion under intermediate scrutiny.

                                                        B

Petitioners’ counterarguments are unpersuasive. Petitioners contend that Texas could
adopt less restrictive means of protecting children, such as encouraging parents to install
content-filtering software on their children’s devices or requiring internet service providers
to block adult content unless a household opts in to receiving it. But, even assuming these
approaches are equally or more effective, under intermediate scrutiny a “regulation will not
be invalid simply because a court concludes that the government’s interest could be
adequately served by some less-speech-restrictive alternative.” Texas’s interest in shielding
children from sexual content “ ‘would be achieved less effectively absent’” H. B. 1181, and it
cannot be said that “a substantial portion of the burden” that H. B. 1181 imposes fails “to
advance [Texas’s] goals.” That is enough to show that the Texas Legislature adequately
tailored H. B. 1181, regardless of whether some other approach might be superior.14

Petitioners further argue that H. B. 1181 is not appropriately tailored, because it does not
require age verification on other sites, such as search engines and social-media websites,
where children are likely to find sexually explicit content. But, under intermediate scrutiny,
“ ‘the First Amendment imposes no freestanding underinclusiveness limitation,’” and Texas
“ ‘need not address all aspects of a problem in one fell swoop.’” Further, Texas has a
reasonable basis for excluding these sites from H. B. 1181’s coverage. The statute does not
contain any special exception for social-media sites. Rather, such sites fall outside the
statute to the extent that less than a third of their content is obscene to minors. And, it is
reasonable for Texas to conclude that websites with a higher proportion of sexual content
are more inappropriate for children to visit than those with a lower proportion. The statute,
on the other hand, does explicitly exempt search engines. But, search engines do not
exercise the same degree of control over the websites to which they link, so the State could
reasonably conclude that it makes less sense to regulate them.

14 Petitioners contend that H. B. 1181 does not allow covered websites to use newer biometric methods of age

verification, like face scans, that they claim are less likely to give rise to privacy concerns. Texas disagrees,
maintaining that H. B. 1181 does allow such methods. We need not resolve this disagreement because Texas is
not required to adopt the least restrictive means of advancing its interests to pass intermediate scrutiny. It is
sufficient that verifying age by government identification and transactional data is a legitimate legislative
choice that does not impose excessive burdens on users.



                                                       287.
Petitioners next assert that privacy concerns and the unique stigma surrounding
pornography will make age verification too chilling for adults. But, users only have to
submit verification to the covered website itself or the third-party service with which the
website contracts. Both those entities have every incentive to assure users of their privacy.
In any event, the use of pornography has always been the subject of social stigma. This
social reality has never been a reason to exempt the pornography industry from otherwise
valid regulation. And, the decades-long history of some pornographic websites requiring age
verification refutes any argument that the chill of verification is an insurmountable
obstacle for users.

                                              ***

H. B. 1181 simply requires adults to verify their age before they can access speech that is
obscene to children. It is therefore subject only to intermediate scrutiny, which it readily
survives. The statute advances the State’s important interest in shielding children from
sexually explicit content. And, it is appropriately tailored because it permits users to verify
their ages through the established methods of providing government-issued identification
and sharing transactional data. The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
is affirmed.

[Justice Kagan’s dissent omitted]

                                  NOTES AND QUESTIONS

Justice Thomas’ opinion is an extraordinarily complicated opinion that relies heavily on
innuendo and omissions. It needs multiple careful readings to fully appreciate everything it
says and doesn’t say. The following notes and questions will highlight some of the
innuendos and omissions. (If you want a deeper dive, Justice Kagan’s dissent also
highlights some of the innuendo and omissions).

Don’t overlook the majority’s bottom-line conclusion: the majority fully understands that
their opinion will prevent publishers from publishing constitutionally protected content to
readers who (as admitted by the majority) everyone agrees that the constitution permits to
receive that content. And yet, the majority says it doesn’t care. Thus, the majority endorses
the inevitable censorship effectuated by H.B. 1181. Indeed, the leading pornography
website, Pornhub, already exited the Texas market entirely due to H.B. 1181. See William
Mehado, Pornhub Suspends Site in Texas Due to State’s Age-Verification Law, TEXAS
TRIBUNE (Mar. 14, 2024), https://www.texastribune.org/2024/03/14/texas-pornhub-5th-
circuit-age-verification-paxton/.

Internet Exceptionalism. This opinion squarely raises the original Internet Law
exceptionalism question: how is the Internet unique, special, or different compared to the
offline world? The FSC majority treats online and offline age authentication as equivalent,
but this is clearly a false equivalency.

First, many of the offline age authentication mandates cited by Justice Thomas don’t
restrict the distribution of speech. There are minimal or no speech consequences from
restricting minors’ access to cigarettes, liquor, lottery tickets, or fireworks. In contrast, the


                                               288.
Texas law has major speech consequences; it unambiguously restricts speech for both
adults and minors. Furthermore, if regulated websites allow users to upload content, the
Texas law blocks users from speaking, not just reading.

Second, online age authentication works differently than offline age authentication in
numerous significant ways, such as:

      Offline age authentication doesn’t impose any marginal costs on the authenticator,
       such as a store clerk checking ID before completing a restricted transaction. In
       contrast, online publishers will incur substantial costs to set up an authentication
       system and likely will incur further substantial costs to complete each individual
       authentication. Publishers must find a way to bear these marginal costs, if they can.
      Retailers complying with the law at issue in Ginsberg didn’t have to authenticate
       their customers until a buyer attempted to purchase a restricted item (and any
       authentication could be done visually in an instant unless the buyer wasn’t clearly
       too old or too young). In contrast, the Texas law requires publishers to authenticate
       readers’ ages before the readers can access the website at all. It’s like a bookstore
       imposing a barrier to access at the entry door before potential customers could enter
       the premises, instead of doing the authentication only when a specific buyer is
       trying to make a restricted purchase. This barrier to entry discourages casual
       readers, especially because the reader will need to spend some time to complete the
       authentication. In contrast to offline retail shoppers, online readers are highly
       intolerant of small delays—even a few extra seconds—that impede their ability to
       reach their desired destination. Thus, by imposing the authentication process at an
       earlier stage online, the Texas law increases the number of readers who will decide
       not to access the publishers’ websites at all, even if they are legally entitled to do so.
      The earlier authentication also means the publisher must incur any marginal
       authentication costs before the publisher knows if the reader will generate any
       revenues for them. These costs will especially impact publishers who have a small
       fraction of minor readers. If only 1% of the publisher’s readers are minors, the
       publisher must nevertheless pay the authentication costs to confirm that the other
       99% of its readers are adults.
      Offline age authentication typically doesn’t create any records of the authentication
       information. For example, in Ginsberg, the restricted retailers won’t make or keep a
       photocopy of the buyer’s government ID. In contrast, online age authentication
       necessarily must generate and transmit electronic records of users’ highly sensitive
       information to transfer the information from the user’s device to the authenticator’s
       servers. H.B. 1181 says authenticators “may not retain any identifying information
       of the individual,” and authenticators will promise to adhere to good data practices
       even if not required by law. However, if readers worry that their data will be
       captured or intercepted despite the law and any promises, they will still balk at
       navigating the age authentication process, which again denies adult readers access
       to constitutionally protected material.

For a fuller discussion of the differences between online and offline age authentication, see
Eric Goldman, The “Segregate-and-Suppress” Approach to Regulating Child Safety Online,
28 STAN. TECH. L. REV. 173 (2025).




                                              289.
Did the majority’s intermediate scrutiny analysis adequately account for these differences?

Reconsider the majority’s assertion that “Applying the more demanding strict-scrutiny
standard would call into question the validity of all age-verification requirements.” If there
are material differences between offline and online age authentication, would it?

And when the majority says “Strict scrutiny therefore cannot apply to laws, such as in-
person age-verification requirements, which are traditional, widespread, and not thought to
raise a significant First Amendment issue”—notice the passive voice in the last clause. Who
thinks that, and isn’t that assuming the conclusion that the majority is trying to justify?

COPA and H.B. 1181, Compared. The Texas legislature clearly hoped to overturn the Reno
v. ACLU and Ashcroft v. ACLU precedents. Instead of innovating some novel way of
restricting minor access to online pornography, the Texas legislative drafters essentially
cloned-and-revised the Child Online Protection Act from 1998. As a result, the Texas
legislature tendered a variation of COPA to the Supreme Court, with the hope that the
Supreme Court would reach a different outcome than it did the first time (which it did).

How did the majority distinguish COPA from H.B. 1181? The majority says that COPA was
a content ban, whereas H.B. 1181 only restricts, not bans, content because the state must
prove the defendant’s failure to age authenticate rather than treating age authentication as
an affirmative defense. (The passage: “COPA established an age-verification defense. But,
because it did so only as an affirmative defense, COPA still operated as a ban on the public
posting of material that is obscene to minors… The same is not true under H. B. 1181,
which makes the lack of age verification an element that the State must plead and prove.”)
Does that distinction persuade you that H.B. 1181 should be subject to intermediate
scrutiny instead of the strict scrutiny applied to COPA?

This Opinion is Calvinball* (Many Times Over). The majority opinion made many novel and
dubious jurisprudential moves that will either disrupt First Amendment jurisprudence or
prove to be one-off results-driven exceptions. Some examples:

* Characterizing “obscene as to minors” content as “partially protected content.”
Traditionally, speech is either constitutionally protected or it’s not; the Supreme Court has
enumerated a small list of content categories (such as obscenity) that are categorically
ineligible for First Amendment protection; those exceptions have been tightly defined to
minimize their scope (such as the Miller test defining obscenity narrowly and precisely);
and the Supreme Court has regularly refused to designate additional categories of content
that are outside the scope of the First Amendment. For example, the Supreme Court
refused to classify videos of people crushing animals to death as unprotected by the First
Amendment. See United States v. Stevens, 559 U.S. 460 (2010).

So long as a content category qualified for First Amendment protection, the Court would
then determine the level of scrutiny based on the nature of the restriction, i.e., a


* The term “Calvinball” comes from the Calvin and Hobbes comic strip. There is only one permanent rule in

Calvinball: players cannot play it the same way twice. In the Trump era, “Calvinball” has become a metaphor
for the disregard of the rule of law.



                                                     290.
time/place/manner restriction would receive more relaxed scrutiny than a viewpoint-based
restriction.

In this opinion, the majority instead says that “obscene as to minors” content is “partially”
protected content, whatever that means. This leads to baffling statements like: “Because
speech that is obscene to minors is unprotected to the extent that the State imposes only an
age-verification requirement, H. B. 1181’s content-based restriction does not require strict
scrutiny.” Doesn’t this statement assume the conclusion it is nominally trying to prove?

If the “partially protected content” classification option is here to stay, it’s possible many
more content categories to receive that classification and some lesser level of scrutiny—
which will become an open invitation for legislatures to dramatically expand their
censorship efforts.

* The majority’s distinction between content “bans” and content “restrictions” for purposes
of establishing the level of scrutiny.

First, traditionally the Court would equally treat both bans and restrictions as forms of
censorship, although a ban might have fared worse under the applicable level of scrutiny
than a lighter “restriction.”

Second, H.B. 1181 acts as a categorical ban on minors accessing “obscene as to minor”
content from certain online publishers (and, as mentioned above, those bans also block
minors from authoring content on the regulated websites). So while the website publishers
are not “banned” from publishing their content, millions of Texan children are still
categorically banned from receiving content. Does the majority adequately acknowledge
this consequence when characterizing the law as “not a ban”?

Third, any adults who cannot successfully navigate the age authentication barrier are also
blocked from accessing constitutionally protected material they are constitutionally
permitted to access. For example, many adult Texans do not have government-issued IDs
and may be unable to authenticate their ages. Perhaps you don’t personally know adults
without government-issued IDs, but in 2020, nearly 30 million US adults did not have a
non-expired driver’s license. Also, if the authenticator misclassifies an adult as a minor,
that person might not be able to correct that misclassification, which will then categorically
block the adult from accessing the publisher. The majority’s characterizations of H.B. 1181
as a content restriction, not a ban, disregard the real-world impacts that online age
authentication will have on many adult Texans.

Perhaps the majority’s dubious distinction between bans vs. restrictions is best exemplified
by the majority’s mischaracterization of precedent. The majority explained: “we did so to
invalidate “a blanket ban” on broadcasting “indecent” but “not ... obscene” cable television
channels between the hours of 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. Playboy, 529 U.S., at 808. In contrast, H.
B. 1181 is not a blanket prohibition.” However, a restriction on the permissible timing of
broadcasting indecent content plainly isn’t a “blanket ban.” The regulation left open times
of the day the content could be broadcast, so it’s a time, place, or manner restriction. By
mischaracterizing the prior broadcasting law as a “blanket ban,” the majority created a
false distinction between H.B. 1181 and the precedent.



                                               291.
* Setting the level of scrutiny as intermediate scrutiny. In Ginsberg, the Supreme Court—
applying rational basis scrutiny—approved of a state law that restricted commercial
entities from selling pornography to minors. How does the majority maneuver from that
precedent to find that the Texas law should be evaluated using intermediate scrutiny?

The majority claims: “The only principled way to give due consideration to both the First
Amendment and States’ legitimate interests in protecting minors is to employ a less
exacting standard.” Is the majority saying that every time the state articulates a laudable
policy interest, the law warrants less exacting scrutiny? This blows apart the traditional
scrutiny setting level, where the strength of the state’s interest is considered as part of
applying the scrutiny. The majority seems to suggest that the strength of a state’s interest
doublecounts towards both determining the scrutiny level and applying the scrutiny level.
This isn’t how the Supreme Court has traditionally done its First Amendment analyses.

Further, how does the majority justify treating H.B. 1181 as not a “content-based” law
(which would trigger strict scrutiny) when the law imposes the age authentication
obligation only for one content category? Historically, laws that disadvantaged one content
category were “content-based” laws. The majority acknowledges but sidesteps this issue by
saying that obscene as to minors content isn’t covered by the First Amendment at all. But if
that were true, the scrutiny level should be rational basis.

* neither of the lower courts in this case conducted an intermediate scrutiny analysis. The
lower court applied strict scrutiny per Reno v. ACLU and Ashcroft v. ACLU, and the Fifth
Circuit applied rational-basis scrutiny per Ginsberg. As a result, the majority conducted its
intermediate scrutiny analysis de novo, rather than reviewing and responding to a lower
court’s intermediate scrutiny analysis. Plus, the litigants did not get the chance to fully
brief and present additional fact evidence to guide the intermediate scrutiny analysis.
Historically, when the Supreme Court reversed lower courts to conclude that intermediate
scrutiny applied, it would have considered remanding the case to the lower courts to
conduct the intermediate scrutiny review in the first instance, subject to a subsequent
review by the Supreme Court if needed. Some problems with the majority’s intermediate
scrutiny analysis may be attributable to its de novo effort.

Countermoves to the Texas Statute? Texas H.B. 1181 applies only when a “commercial
entity…knowingly and intentionally publishes or distributes material on an Internet
website, including a social media platform, more than one-third of which is sexual material
harmful to minors.” It’s not clear how the 1/3 fraction is computed, but regardless,
publishers could satisfy this standard by expanding the unrestricted content to its database
sufficient to drop below the statutory threshold. For example, an adult content website
could use Generative AI to produce lots of worthless non-adult content items, upload the
junky content to their database (knowing that no one will ever see it or care), and no longer
be subject to the law. Would that countermove benefit society generally or any minors?
Does this possible countermove cast doubts about whether the law is “sufficiently tailored
to Texas’s interest”?

Age “Verification” Glossary

The term “age verification” is semantically ambiguous. Sometimes it’s used to describe a
specific type of age authentication; other times, it’s the generic descriptor for all


                                             292.
authentication options. To sidestep this semantic ambiguity, I instead use the term “age
authentication” to describe the genre, and I use the following terms for more specific
meanings:

      “Age assurance” means that a reader is confirmed as an adult and not a minor,
       without any further precision about the person’s age.
      “Age estimation” means that the reader’s age is estimated within a margin of error,
       e.g., within a range of plus or minus two years. The term “age assessment” is
       sometimes used.
      “Age verification” means that a reader’s exact age is determined.

The terms “age-gating,” “self declaration,” “age declaration,” or “self attestation” refer to
asking users to self-report their ages. Self-reporting is not considered a reliable method of
age authentication because users can easily lie.

How Is Age Authenticated?

There are many ways to authenticate users’ ages online, but the EFF has explained:

       [Authentication] methods don’t each fit somewhere on a spectrum of “more
       safe” and “less safe,” or “more accurate” and “less accurate.” Rather, they
       each fall on a spectrum of “dangerous in one way” to “dangerous in a different
       way.” . . . [E]very solution has serious privacy, accuracy, or security problems.

The two primary authentication methods today are visual inspections (such as a face scan
that estimates the person’s age) and document review, such as uploading a person’s
government-issued ID. Both of these methods have many serious downsides. For example,
scans of people’s biometric information exposes highly sensitive and immutable physical
attributes to strangers, who may aspire to use that information for nefarious purposes. And
many adults don’t have government-issued IDs; and government-issued IDs also contain
highly sensitive information beyond the person’s age (such as address, height, weight, etc.)
that are attractive to malefactors.

Worse, both authentication methods are gamable. There is an active black market for
materials that defeat face scans and government ID-based authentications.

H.B. 1181 allows age authentication via two methods: (1) government-issued IDs, or (2) “a
commercially reasonable method that relies on public or private transactional data to verify
the age of an individual.” “Transactional data” is defined as “a sequence of information that
documents an exchange, agreement, or transfer between an individual, commercial entity,
or third party used for the purpose of satisfying a request or event. The term includes
records from mortgage, education, and employment entities.” No one knows for sure what
the transactional data-based authentication means, and its definition does not seem to
include face scans. As a result, most publishers will rely on government-issued IDs to
comply with the Texas law.

There are many other potential authentication methods beyond face scans and government-
issued IDs, such as (this list is not comprehensive):



                                              293.
      Capacity testing. The authenticator can ask the user to answer questions or perform
       tasks that only adults should be able to complete.
      Social vouching, where other users vouch for the age of a user.
      Data mining. Services can look into a user’s past online activity and characterize it
       as more like what adults do or what minors do.
      Credit cards. The CDA and COPA both specified that an online publisher could treat
       a user as an adult if they presented a valid credit card number. This approach is
       considered not credible today because many minors have credit cards.

Recall the EFF’s caution: there is no better or worse age authentication option; they are all
problematic, just in different ways. For more details on the problems with each of these
options, see Eric Goldman, The “Segregate-and-Suppress” Approach to Regulating Child
Safety Online, 28 STAN. TECH. L. REV. 173 (2025).

Who Does the Age Authentication?

A related question is: who should do the age authentication? Texas H.B. 1181 allows the
publisher to do it themselves or to outsource the authentication to a third-party vendor.
Some other age authentication laws don’t permit the publisher to do the authentication
themselves out of fear that the publisher will collect the users’ data and use the data
against the user’s interests later or sell the data to third parties. Even if the law permits
them to authenticate their users, many publishers won’t want to do the authentication
themselves because it’s complex and not part of their business’ core focus. As a result, most
publishers will rely on third-party authenticators.

If constituents have installed digital government IDs on their devices, authentication can
be done using “zero-knowledge proofs.” Intermediary software located on a user’s device
receives a publisher’s age authentication request, checks the digital government ID, and
responds to the publisher only with a yes/no about the user’s age. However, the label “zero-
knowledge proof” is misleading; it refers to the publisher not gaining unnecessary
information about the user, but other players in the system know a lot about the user.
Given how many adults don’t have physical-space government-issued IDs, it may be a while
before digital government IDs are sufficiently prevalent for this system to solve any
problem.

Some governments are now requiring app stores to authenticate the age of their app store
users and then either block users from accessing apps that the government doesn’t permit
for minors or convey the information to app makers so they can restrict access to minors.
App-level authentication is at best an incomplete solution because users can install apps in
other ways that bypass any authentication requirement. Nevertheless, Facebook has been
pushing this solution (as a way of making someone else do the authentication work); Google
and Apple have been resisting it. Note that if app store authentication becomes prevalent,
Google and Apple could decide to turn the authentication information into a lucrative
business by charging an authentication fee for every app download—essentially a way of
taxing a lot of standard Internet activities. Both Apple and Google have already taken
moves in this direction.




                                             294.
If policymakers require online age authentication, the adult content industry generally
prefers device-level authentication. If adult content websites can check whether or not the
device has been authenticated as being used by an adult, then it’s not hard to block
unauthenticated devices. However, device-level authentication has some obvious problems,
including: adults and minors may share the same device (like a parent and child); an adult
may falsely authenticate a child’s device for any number of reasons; and a black market of
adult-authenticated devices would emerge.

Maybe all of these problems with who does the authentication and how it’s done will be
solved eventually, but policymakers imposing online age authentication mandates haven’t
solved them today, and that creates a lot of risk for publishers and ambiguity for users
right now. Do you think that the FSC v. Paxton majority’s intermediate scrutiny analysis
properly accounted for these problems?

Are Other Age Authentication Laws Constitutional?

As the majority mentions, states have enacted a wide range of laws that impose mandatory
online age authentication beyond “pornography” websites or access to “obscene as to
minors” material. What does the majority opinion indicate about the constitutionality of age
authentication mandates in other circumstances?

The opinion depends heavily on the Texas law’s claim to target “obscene as to minors”
content. Arguably other laws would not trigger intermediary scrutiny if they target content
that is “fully” protected by the First Amendment as opposed to “partially protected.”
However, the majority seems pretty supportive of age authentication for any law that
purports to protect minors. For example, the majority says that “adults have no First
Amendment right to avoid age verification.” If that’s true, then the majority might uphold
age authentication mandates beyond the “obscene as to minors” context. The majority also
treats age authentication as an inherent necessity for any legislative efforts to protect
children online. That suggests that the majority could legitimatize age authentication for
any category of content a legislature seeks to restrict, because the restrictive law can’t work
without age authentication.

We’ll get more answers soon enough. A number of other age authentication mandates are
heading to the Supreme Court imminently.

Mandatory Online Age Authentication is Bad Policy

Regardless of its constitutionality, the imposition of mandatory online age authentication
will have dramatic and negative consequences for adults, children, publishers, the Internet,
and society generally.

Some of the negative consequences include:

      As discussed above, online age authentication requires the overdisclosure of highly
       sensitive and private information, and that in turn creates additional security risks
       from the potential collection, use, disclosure, or interception of such information.




                                              295.
      The interposition of an authentication process will slow down readers’ access to the
       content they seek. Instead of following a seamless “web” of content, readers will be
       constantly prompted to navigate through an authentication process fraught with
       privacy and security risks. Today, you are used to clicking on a link and going. In the
       future, clicking on a link will likely bring you to an age authentication “wall” that
       you will have to surmount to get to your goal. Knowing of the looming access
       barriers, many readers will stop clicking on links so freely, directing their
       readership instead to publishers they already know and have a relationship with.
       This works to the disadvantage of new marketplace entrants who haven’t built up
       their readership and haven’t earned readers’ trust yet.
      In addition to readers’ concerns about privacy and security risks, the time delay will
       increase the “bounce” rate of readers, who will turn around, rather than take the
       time to navigate through the authentication process. In the adult content field, the
       bounce rates from an age authentication process can be 90%+, partially reflecting
       users’ heightened privacy issues. But any process that delays or slows down readers’
       access to online content will increase bounce rates substantially. In this way, age
       authentication mandates shrink publishers’ audiences and revenues.
      Publishers also have to pay to authenticate all readers—even if, as discussed above,
       the readers will never generate any revenues for the publisher. Some publishers can
       absorb those costs. Other publishers will have to change their business models to
       fund the costs, such as switching from an ad-supported service to a paywalled
       service. Publishers who can’t afford the costs likely will exit the industry. So online
       age authentication mandates are likely to reduce the amount of free content, and
       shift the remaining content behind paywalls. This exacerbates digital divides; and to
       the extent readers will only pay for a limited number of paywalled databases, it will
       encourage market consolidation into a smaller number of larger players.

Combining these dynamics, online age authentication mandates increase publisher costs
and are likely to shrink the size of publishers’ audience and revenues. Higher costs and
smaller revenues will reshape the information ecosystem and categorically reduce the
availability of constitutionally protected content, especially free content. In other words,
intentionally or not, online age authentication mandates will affect marketplace
competition, the ability of new entrants to succeed, and industry consolidation.

If we were only talking about “porn sites,” some people might nevertheless accept these
consequences as the cost of protecting children online. But legislatures have imposed the
mandates on publishers far outside the porn context. For example, the California Age-
Appropriate Design Code Act—currently enjoined by lower courts for violating the First
Amendment, but will that last after FSC v. Paxton?—imposes online age authentication on
most larger commercial websites. That includes business-to-business websites that pose no
real risk to children and services that allow users to talk with each other, thus inhibiting
the ability of minors (and adults) to author content online.

In addition to blocking some authors from getting access to publishing tools, online age
authentication mandates chill or censor online speech in other ways. Publishers are more
likely to require readers to establish persistent accounts that require users to login (so the
publisher doesn’t have to keep paying to authenticate the same reader). In the process,
however, the readers lose even more privacy. Persistent accounts will also discourage



                                              296.
potential authors, such as whistleblowers, who only feel comfortable speaking up on an
unattributable basis. Governments may not stop at age authentication mandates; they may
also impose identity authentication mandates too (sometimes called “Know Your
Customer,” or KYC). Identity authentication further chills readership and speech, and it
also provides an infrastructure for the government to force publishers to impose blocklists
on targeted individuals. This can lead to dystopian outcomes like the government picking-
and-choosing who gets to read what. Even without that level of dystopia, some advocates of
mandatory online age authentication have made their censorship goals clear. They want to
depopulate all pornography from the Internet for both minors and adults (despite it being
constitutionally protected for adults); or they take increasingly expansive views of what’s
objectionable for minors, such as categorizing LGBTQ-themed content as “harmful to
minors” as a way of trying to censor that entire content genre.

Finally, courts routinely accept the premise that online age authentication mandates
protect children online, but that assumption deserves critical scrutiny. The harsh reality is
that the mandates, especially when imposed as “one-size-fits-all” mandates that treats all
minors as if they have identical circumstances, will routinely harm children—a
counterproductive and cruelly ironic outcome.

First, due to the privacy and security risks, a minor’s decision to submit their data for
authentication is a complex decision—exactly the kind of complex decisionmaking that
minors aren’t ready for, yet they may be asked to do it repeatedly. Second, minors will
suffer in a reconfigured Internet where there are a smaller number of publishers operating
increasingly behind paywalls. Minors will be able to access less content, and the digital
divides will systematically disadvantage the underprivileged. Third, minors will lose access
to spaces where they can author content, so they will have less of a say on important topics
where their voice is needed to inform policymaking. Fourth, to the extent that minors are
banned from online resources until they become adults, they won’t accumulate the
resiliency needed to use those resources. Minors routinely say that they want to learn how
to use the Internet wisely rather than be shielded from the risks. Essentially, these minors
will be less prepared for the digital future they face as adults.

Most importantly, restrictions to online resources may advantage some minor
subpopulations and disadvantage other subpopulations. This is easiest to see with a
resource like social media. Social media can be harmful to some minors, such as those who
are exposed to harmful content or who become “addicted” to the detriment of other values in
their lives. For other minors, social media makes their lives better, such as for LGBTQ
teens in rural areas who may not have local access to a safe offline community that allows
them to explore and understand their identity. A categorical restriction on minors’ access to
social media doesn’t inherently benefit every minor. Instead, policymakers prioritize the
interests of some minors at the expense of other minors. Worse, usually the policymakers
aren’t transparent about the fact that some minors that will be harmed by the online age
authentication mandate, which silently erases those minors and the harms they will suffer.

These kinds of negative consequences for minor subpopulations is highly relevant to the
constitutional scrutiny of the mandate. It may demonstrate that the law’s proponents are
only making pretextual claims about actually benefiting children, or that the means they
chose don’t accomplish that purported goal. Did the FSC v. Paxton majority’s approach to



                                             297.
intermediate scrutiny show sufficient awareness of and sensitivity to the risks that the law
might harm some children?

Due to widespread interests in improving children’s welfare, “protect kids online” laws can
become a “Trojan horse” for policymakers to advance goals that have nothing to do with
protecting children because constituents and advocates will instinctively support any bill
that claims to improve child safety (even if it won’t). It’s deeply troubling when
policymakers use children as political props to hide their real agendas, and yet it’s an
integral part of how Internet Law is developing today.

Age Authentication in Private Litigation. Increasingly, private litigants claim that, even if
there’s no legislation mandating it, Internet services should be liable for not adopting age
authentication to protect their minor users. Prior to FSC, most courts were rejecting these
arguments. See, e.g., Doe (K.B.) v. Backpage.com, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1057 (N.D. Cal.
2025):

       Doe’s theory of liability derives from Meta’s alleged failure to include
       adequate age and identity verification measures that would prevent the
       creation of fake accounts facilitating sex trafficking communications…the
       duty cuts to the core of Meta’s role as a publisher: that is, determining who
       can and cannot speak on its platform. Doe’s proposed verification
       requirements are designed with the particular purpose of limiting who will
       create an Instagram account, and more specifically, limiting the types of
       content likely to be posted from those accounts (i.e., sex trafficking content).
       A platform’s decision as to whether to allow anonymous speech, and the
       consequent effects on the content of the speech that proliferates on the
       platform, is a classic publication decision. It is a determination of who may
       speak, and thus, whose content may be barred on the platform.

See also Doe v. Grindr, LLC, 2025 N.Y. Misc. LEXIS 1942 (N.Y. Supreme Ct. 2025). Will
FSC change these rulings?




                                              298.
                             A Note on the Take It Down Act

In 2025, Congress enacted the “Take It Down” Act. The law has two main provisions. First,
it criminalizes the non-consensual distribution of certain “intimate visual depictions,”
including realistic depictions generated by AI. When minors are depicted, these restrictions
partially overlap existing prohibitions on child sexual abuse material (CSAM). However,
the law expands the boundaries of criminalized content.

This note will focus on the law’s second major provision, which imposes a notice-and-
takedown scheme on online publishers. We already encountered notice-and-takedown in
connection with copyright (Section 512) and trademark (Tiffany v. eBay). The Take It Down
Act applies those principles to certain “intimate visual depictions.”

With some exceptions, the law applies to any website or app that publishes third-party
content. Regulated publishers must honor requests to take down “intimate visual
depictions” of the requestor, or their designated agent, and “make reasonable efforts to
identify and remove any known identical copies of such depiction,” all within 48 hours of
receiving the takedown notice. The takedown provisions go into effect in 2026.

Similar to the DMCA’s takedown notice procedures (17 USC 512(c)(3)), the law specifies the
required elements of a takedown notice:

   (i)     a physical or electronic signature of the identifiable individual (or an
           authorized person acting on behalf of such individual);
   (ii)    an identification of, and information reasonably sufficient for the covered
           platform to locate, the intimate visual depiction of the identifiable
           individual;
   (iii)   a brief statement that the identifiable individual has a good faith belief
           that any intimate visual depiction identified under clause (ii) is not
           consensual, including any relevant information for the covered platform
           to determine the intimate visual depiction was published without the
           consent of the identifiable individual; and
   (iv)    information sufficient to enable the covered platform to contact the
           identifiable individual (or an authorized person acting on behalf of such
           individual).

Despite their similarities, these elements are less rigorous than their DMCA analogues.

For example, a 512(c)(3) notice submitter must declare under penalty of perjury that they
are authorized to act on behalf of the copyright owner. There is no similar “perjury” penalty
for Take It Down Act notices submitted without authorization of the depicted individuals.

Also, a 512(c)(3) notice must specify the location of the allegedly infringing material. If the
service removes the specified item, it has satisfied its prerequisites to retain its DMCA safe
harbor. In contrast, the Take It Down Act requires a publisher to affirmatively seek out and
find other “identical” copies of the depictions. Thus, unlike the DMCA, the publisher can
never be 100% confident that it’s removed every item that the law requires it to remove.




                                              299.
The submitter’s declaration of non-consent is also potentially problematic. Will it be
sufficient for the submitter to simply declare in their notice that “I didn’t consent to the
dissemination of this depiction” without any further evidence or confirmation?

In the DMCA, uploaders who disagree with a copyright owner’s takedown notice can submit
a “putback” request (512(g)) that, if the service honors, redirects the parties’ dispute into
court. The Take It Down Act has no similar statutory mechanisms for uploaders to contest
the declaration of non-consent.

Also, the DMCA included a cause of action for bad-faith submission of 512(c)(3) notices
(512(f)). Although most 512(f) cases fail, the Take It Down Act has no 512(f) equivalent.
Without any legal mechanism to discourage the submission of illegitimate Take It Down
Act takedown notices, regulated publishers may be flooded with removal notices. For
example, anti-pornography advocates could easily automate the submission of takedown
notices targeting pornographic depictions, even if the advocates have no legal basis to
submit the notices.

Note: even if the Take It Down Act’s specifications for notices had more closely adhered to
512(c)(3), that wouldn’t solve all of the problems. The DMCA notice-and-takedown scheme
is notorious for unjustified overremovals. The Take It Down Act turbocharges the
overremovals problem.

                                              ***

As evidence of the overremoval risk, consider how a publisher will view a Take It Down
takedown notice it receives. Upon receive, the publisher has a 48 hour window to conduct
some or all of the following investigatory steps before deciding whether or not to make the
removal:

      Can the publisher find the targeted item?
      Is anyone identifiable in the targeted item?
      Is the person submitting the takedown notice one of the people identifiable in the
       targeted item? If not, does the submitter have the requisite authority to submit the
       takedown notice?
      Does the targeted item contain an intimate visual depiction of the submitter?
      Did the submitting person consent to the depiction?
      Is the depiction otherwise subject to some privilege, such as the First Amendment?
      Can the service find other “identical” copies of the targeted item?
      [repeat all of the above steps for each duplicate. Note the duplicates each may
       require a different analysis than the item targeted by the notice. For example, a
       duplicate may be embedded in a different context, such as a still image in a
       documentary, which could lead to a different conclusion.]

Alternatively, instead of undertaking a multi-step, complex, expensive, legally risky, and
likely irresolute investigation for content that the publisher may not value highly, a
publisher could honor every takedown notice and remove any instance of the complained-
about intimate visual depiction it can easily find, without doing any further diligence at all.
If you were running the operations team processing incoming Take It Down takedown



                                              300.
notices, which approach would you choose? In the DMCA context, most publishers have
adopted an “if in doubt, take it down” attitude towards 512(c)(3) notices, because liability
only attaches from continuing to publish the item, not from its removal. The same dynamics
will likely drive publishers to adopt a similar policy for Take It Down Act notices.

Given the potential harms caused by nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, it may be
tempting to accept the overremovals risk as not a significant problem. This is misguided,
both procedurally and substantively.

Procedurally, notice-and-takedown schemes operate extrajudically. The whole point of the
Take It Down Act is to permit people to remove content simply by asking, rather than
requiring them to go to court and make their case to a judge. In effect, the Take It Down
Act structures a dialogue solely between the complainer—who has incentives to lie—and
the publisher—who has incentives to remove items regardless of their legality. This two-
party dialogue intentionally excludes any other relevant parties, such as the uploader,
other people depicted in the targeted item who may want its continued distribution, and
anyone else whose interests may be affected by the continued publication or removal of the
targeted item.

In other words, to save time and money for the complainer, the Take It Down Act bypasses
the due process safeguards built into judicial review of alleged legal violations. But
sacrificing due process ensures higher error rates and inadequate considerations of the
effects of a removal decision on broader social interests.

Substantively, there are circumstances where the continued publication of intimate visual
depictions advances important social values. For example, a depiction may provide
essential proof that the depicted individual engaged in sexual misconduct or has been lying
about their behavior. As a result, the Take It Down Act might make it harder for #MeToo
victims to prove their claims or for whistleblowers to expose politicians’ or celebrities’
misbehavior.

A paradigmatic example of this is Rep. Anthony Weiner, who repeatedly sent unrequested
dick pics to some of his social media followers. After he got caught the first time, he
resigned from Congress. However, he attempted a political comeback, during which
recipients claimed he was still sending unrequested dick pics. Weiner publicly denied this,
but his denials became untenable when the recipients publicly shared the images. Under
the Take It Down Act, Weiner may have been able to suppress those posts and continue to
illegitimately cast doubt on the recipients’ claims, possibly avoiding accountability for his
behavior.

The Take It Down Act delegates enforcement authority for publishers’ compliance with the
law’s procedural mechanisms to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). Designating the
FTC as the Take It Down “cop” is an odd choice. The FTC typically supervises commercial
entities’ marketplace conduct, but this law asks it to review editorial publication decisions
having nothing to do with commercial “trade.” Thus, the law asks the FTC to do something
it has no expertise in doing—essentially turning it into a censorship board.

Worse, the FTC under Chairman Ferguson has repeatedly demonstrated an eagerness to
use the FTC’s discretionary enforcement powers to advance censorship. The Take It Down


                                             301.
Act gives the FTC a powerful tool for its censorship toolkit. The FTC can exercise its
discretionary enforcement to put extraordinary pressure on a disfavored publisher, such as
by alleging that the publisher took longer than 48 hours to remove an item or failed to
reasonably identify and remove identical copies. Whether the FTC’s allegations are true or
not, the FTC can easily use the threat of substantial defense costs to extract concessions.

The law’s power is especially apparent by considering the consequences if the FTC
weaponizes the Take It Down Act as a broad-based anti-online pornography law and
demanded publishers’ exacting compliance with the law. This kind of heightened FTC
attention would surely motivate some publishers to block all pornography, consensual or
not, or exit the user-generated content industry entirely.

                                            ***

It’s unclear if and when the Take It Down Act’s notice-and-takedown scheme will be subject
to a First Amendment challenge. When that occurs, what do you think the Supreme Court
will say?

A lot depends on how the Supreme Court characterizes the category of “intimate visual
depictions.” This definition includes content that isn’t only CSAM, and the definition surely
reaches content that would not be characterized as “obscene.” As a result, historically, the
Take It Down Act’s scope would reach content that receives First Amendment protection
and force publishers to stop publishing it. That sounds a lot like impermissible government
censorship.

But as we saw in FSC v. Paxton, the Court created the hybrid category of “partially
protected content” to subject the Texas law to lesser scrutiny; and in the TikTok case, the
Court credited Congress’ alleged concerns about US citizens’ privacy to justify the
restriction. Perhaps the Court will manufacture a way to subject the notice-and-takedown
scheme to something less than strict scrutiny.

If the category of “intimate visual depictions” receives First Amendment protection, at least
in part, the law directly overrides online publishers’ editorial discretion to publish that
constitutionally protected material. (The publishers may voluntarily choose to remove that
content as they wish, but the law erases their discretion). Per the Moody case, the law’s
incursion into the publishers’ editorial discretion regarding constitutionally protected
content looks like a problem.

So the question is: would the current Supreme Court approach this more like FSC/TikTok
or Moody?

Stated differently, Congress has now created two extrajudicial fast lanes for removing
content online: the Take It Down Act for intimate visual depictions and the DMCA for
copyrighted works. This raises the obvious question: why these two categories and not
others? Are intimate visual depictions and copyright the only two categories of content that
justify overriding publishers’ editorial discretion to publish?

Perhaps Congress will progressively expand the categories of content that are subject to an
extrajudicial notice-and-takedown scheme. Who wins, and who loses, if more content items


                                             302.
are forcibly removed extrajudicially? What would the Internet look like if there are dozens
of content categories that are subject to notice-and-takedown?

Alternatively, perhaps the First Amendment’s freedoms of speech and press prevents
Congress from imposing notice-and-takedown for intimate visual depictions or from
expanding notice-and-takedown to other content categories. If so, we might even reconsider
if notice-and-takedown mechanisms are proper for copyright. See Eric Goldman & Jessica
Silbey, Copyright’s Memory Hole, 2019 BYU L. Rev. 929.

In addition to the possible First Amendment conflict, the Take It Down Act nominally
conflicts with Section 230 (discussed shortly), which does not permit a notice-and-takedown
scheme for non-IP content. It remains unclear how courts will resolve that nominal conflict.
As a later-enacted statute, the Take It Down Act might have implicitly amended Section
230. Further, some courts have held that the FTC’s enforcement of the FTC Act
automatically routes around Section 230’s protections. See, e.g., Federal Trade Commission
v. LeadClick Media, LLC, 838 F.3d 158 (2d Cir. 2016). Thus, the Take It Down Act’s
takedown procedures may override the Section 230 default rules.




                                            303.
                       VIII. Defamation and Information Torts

We’ve already discussed several doctrines that expose content publishers to liability,
including copyright, trademark, and various content restrictions such as anti-pornography
laws. This part discusses additional legal risks of publication, including defamation.

In many online publication lawsuits, a common issue is whether online content is meant to
be taken seriously. The next case illustrates the challenges plaintiffs must overcome.

Bauer v. Brinkman, 958 N.W.2d 194 (Iowa 2021)

…Statements that cannot be reasonably interpreted as stating actual facts about a person
are not actionable as defamation. Thus, speech that is considered “rhetorical hyperbole” and
“vigorous epithet” are nonactionable as defamation. Whether a statement is capable of a
defamatory meaning is a question for the court.

We use a four-factor test to determine whether an alleged defamatory statement can
reasonably be interpreted as alleging actual facts or is a protected expression of opinion.
First, we consider “whether the alleged defamatory statement ‘has a precise core of
meaning for which a consensus of understanding exists or, conversely, whether the
statement is indefinite and ambiguous.’” Second, we consider to what degree the statement
is “objectively capable of proof or disproof.” Third, we examine “the context in which the
alleged defamatory statement occurs.” Fourth, we contemplate “the broader social context”
the alleged defamatory statement fits into.

Bauer argues that Brinkman’s speech calling him a slumlord implied a factual assertion
that he is an “unscrupulous landlord” of an apartment building that is a slum or in a slum
area…Brinkman argues that his Facebook comment was a protected expression of opinion.
The dispositive question in this case is whether a reasonable reader could conclude that
Brinkman’s Facebook comment implied a factual statement that Bauer is a rental property
owner or landlord of a slum area.

A statement that is precise and easy to verify is more likely a fact than an opinion. An
example of a defamatory statement that is capable of precise meaning and easily verifiable
is an accusation that a person committed a crime…

When determining whether a statement can reasonably be understood as a factual
assertion we view it “in the context of the surrounding circumstances and within the entire
communication.” The proper inquiry “is not the literal wording of the statement but what a
reasonable reader or listener would have understood the author to have said.” Therefore we
must examine the broader social context the statement was made in, as well as the context
of Brinkman’s specific Facebook comment…

Here, the context of the speech begins with a Facebook post by Gabbie Lynch on her
personal page. The post criticized Bauer for expressing concerns about dog feces outside at
Pet Perfect LLC. Several people commented on her post expressing their own opinions
about Bauer. Bauer concedes in his briefing that none of the comments on the thread
discussed the condition of the apartments or his managerial abilities. It would be more
reasonable for a reader to understand Brinkman’s use of “slumlord” as a serious factual


                                            304.
assertion if the Facebook thread related specifically to Bauer’s occupation and Bauer
Apartments. However, the Facebook post and comments were individual’s emotionally
charged responses to how they perceived Bauer’s actions in relation to Kathy’s business. As
an example of the tone of the comments on the thread, the comment directly above
Brinkman’s states, “Dear Mr. Bauer” followed by a photo with enlarged text stating, “Good
morning. Don’t forget to drink your water and mind your own fucking business.” This
context of an ongoing heated discussion on matters separate from Bauer’s role as a rental
property manager lends support to the conclusion that Brinkman’s speech was name-
calling and an insult rather than an assertion of fact.

An examination of the specific context of Brinkman’s Facebook comment additionally shows
his statements were rhetorical hyperbole rather than assertions of facts. He states “It is
because of shit like this that I need to run for mayor!” followed by a grinning emoji, and
that Bauer is a “PIECE OF SHIT!!!” before calling him a slumlord.* The tone “is pointed,
exaggerated, and heavily laden with emotional rhetoric and moral outrage” thus alerting
readers that the statements are expressions of personal judgment.

Furthermore, Brinkman did not attempt to provide any support for the statement that
Bauer is a slumlord; therefore, a reader is alerted it is an insult and a “single, excited
reference” rather than a factual assertion….

                                        NOTES AND COMMENTS

Elements of a Defamation Claim. Although jurisdictions characterize the required elements
slightly differently, a prima facie case of defamation usually requires the plaintiff to
establish at least the following five elements:

       A statement of fact. A defamatory statement must be capable of being true or false.
        In contrast, an opinion cannot be proved true or false and therefore cannot be
        defamatory. The Bauer case gives some guidance about how to distinguish between
        facts and opinions, but not every jurisdiction will use this four-factor test.
       The statement is false. A true statement, even if damaging or disparaging, is not
        defamatory.
       The statement is defamatory. The statement must injure the plaintiff’s reputation.
        Some statements—such as a claim that a person has a sexually transmitted
        disease—are considered defamation per se, and injury to reputation is presumed.
       The statement is of and concerning the plaintiff. The statement must refer to the
        plaintiff.
       The statement is published to a third party. Communication of the statement to any
        third party constitutes “publication” for this element.

The plaintiff typically bears the burden of proof to establish each of these prima facie
elements. If the plaintiff satisfies that burden, the burden shifts to the defendant to
establish any affirmative defenses.

* [Editor’s note: Brinkman’s complete Facebook post: “It is because of shit like this that I need to run for mayor!

[grinning emoji] Mr. Bauer . . . you sir are a PIECE OF SHIT!!! Let’s not sugar coat things here people. Kathy
Lynch runs a respectable business in this town! You sir are nothing more than a Slum Lord! Period. I would
love to have you walk across the street to the east of your ooh so precious property and discuss this with me!”]



                                                        305.
Libel v. Slander. Historically, defamation law distinguished between oral defamation
(“slander”) and written defamation (“libel”). Though courts still occasionally reference these
distinctions, the modern caselaw has largely mooted this distinction. Courts routinely refer
to “defamation” instead of “slander” or “libel,” and courts often apply the same legal
standards regardless of how the statements were expressed.

Rough Speech Is the Internet’s Norm. Courts routinely treat online speech as more
hyperbolic or opinion-like than they might in other speech venues. For example, Spencer v.
Glover, 397 P.3d 780 (Utah Ct. App. 2017) involved a client’s negative online review of an
attorney. The court said:

       Glover’s review was posted on yelp.com, a website where people post business
       reviews, commenting on their experiences and degrees of satisfaction with
       particular businesses. The district court determined that ‘a necessarily
       subjective online review of a particular business, published in the review
       section of a website commonly used by customers to rank their experiences
       with businesses of all kinds,’ indicates that the statements were an
       expression of opinion….The presence of Glover’s objectionable statements in
       an online review platform signals to readers that he was communicating his
       negative opinion about Spencer.

See also Rosa v. Eaton, 2024 WL 3161853 (S.D.N.Y. 2024): “Online fora, such as Instagram,
are informal, unedited, and typically regarded as fora for stating opinions.”

Hyperlinks as Citations. A number of courts have rejected defamation claims when the
allegedly defamatory statements were accompanied by hyperlinks to sources supporting
that position. In general, the courts treat the allegedly defamatory statement as an opinion
characterizing the factual content of the hyperlinked citation. See, e.g., Adelson v. Harris,
133 Nev. 512 (Nev. Sup. Ct. 2017); Ayyadurai v. Floor64, Inc., 270 F. Supp. 3d 343 (D.
Mass. 2017); Redmond v. Gawker Media LLC, 2012 WL 3243507 (Cal. App. Ct. 2012);
Seldon v. Compass Restaurant, 2012 WL 5363518 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2012).
